NVDA.bottleneck_description: Rated on whether a customer can leave NVIDIA. A substitute for its chips exists (hyperscaler in-house silicon, AMD's merchant parts), so the position is not CRITICAL. But leaving means abandoning CUDA, the software a business runs on, and NVIDIA's interconnect (NVLink, InfiniBand, Spectrum-X) that binds tens of thousands of chips into one machine; rewriting the software and rebuilding the wiring is a multi-year, multi-billion switch. Customers can go elsewhere, and the cost keeps most in place, which is what HIGH means.
NVDA.robotnik_notes: The gravitational centre of the frontier stack. NVIDIA's compute silicon enables robotics inference, satellite processing, and autonomous systems. CoWoS packaging capacity is the binding constraint.

TSM.bottleneck_description: Rated on whether a chip designer can take its most advanced work elsewhere. A substitute exists, since Samsung and Intel run advanced foundries, so the position is not CRITICAL; TSMC is the framework's own leading-edge-foundry archetype for HIGH. Moving to a less advanced foundry means a slower, less efficient chip, and requalifying a design there is a multi-year, multi-billion undertaking with a worse product at the end. Customers can leave and almost none do, which is what HIGH means.
TSM.robotnik_notes: Single most critical node in the frontier stack. Manufactures >90% of the world’s leading-edge logic chips. $165B US investment reshapes geographic risk but creates new Materials demand.

AVGO.bottleneck_description: Rated on whether a customer can work around Broadcom, and it can. Its custom-ASIC advantage is capability rather than control: the work is hard and few do it well, but a customer can move to Marvell, bring more of the design in-house, or fall back on buying NVIDIA's chips. Broadcom owns no software lock-in, no unique manufacturing, and no essential machine, so if it faltered budgets would slip and roadmaps would move by a year or more, but the work would move rather than stop. A company others prefer rather than one they depend on, which is what MEDIUM means.
AVGO.robotnik_notes: Custom ASIC business with a handful of major hyperscaler customers diversifies AI compute beyond GPUs. VMware acquisition adds software layer.

ASML.bottleneck_description: Rated on whether a chipmaker can find its machines elsewhere, and it cannot. ASML is the sole maker of EUV lithography, with no second source, no rival near a working alternative, and no way to make leading-edge chips without these machines, at any price on any timeline. A chipmaker cannot switch, wait, or improvise around it. That is no substitute at all, the step beyond HIGH's costly-but-possible substitute, which makes ASML the framework's own archetype for CRITICAL.
ASML.robotnik_notes: Sole supplier of EUV lithography, the most critical single-source dependency in the entire frontier stack. No alternative exists. Its order book runs years ahead.

MU.bottleneck_description: Peak position is HBM (peak-position ruling: rated on HBM, not the broader DRAM/NAND book). HBM has three qualified makers and Micron is the smallest and most substitutable at ~19-21%, third behind SK Hynix (~50-63%); a customer can transfer to SK Hynix or Samsung at a qualification cost of months, which is the MEDIUM definition. The industry-wide sold-out condition raises switching cost (hence not LOW) but is a cyclical market state, not a permanent feature (hence not HIGH). Anchors the HBM spread: SK Hynix HIGH when built, Samsung between, Micron MEDIUM as the smallest of three.
MU.robotnik_notes: HBM memory capacity gates AI accelerator production. FY2025 revenue $37.4bn, up 49%, with HBM a fast-growing slice. HBM4 shipping for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin.

AMD.robotnik_notes: MI300X validates multi-vendor AI accelerator demand. Data Center segment exceeded $14B, broadening compute supply for robotics.

LRCX.robotnik_notes: Etch and deposition equipment essential for advanced node manufacturing. Benefits from every fab expansion globally.

AMAT.robotnik_notes: Gate-all-around and advanced packaging equipment driving growth. Essential for next-gen AI chips for robotics applications.

INTC.robotnik_notes: Foundry pivot critical for US semiconductor sovereignty. 18A customer wins validate CHIPS Act thesis. If IFS succeeds, reduces Taiwan concentration.

KLAC.robotnik_notes: Process control and metrology — defect inspection critical for sub-3nm yield management. Benefits from increasing process complexity.

ISRG.robotnik_notes: $8.9B revenue, 20M procedures. da Vinci 5 platform. Razor-and-blade model template for robotics commercialisation. 57% recurring revenue.

6861 JP.robotnik_notes: Factory automation bellwether with 50%+ margins. Machine vision sensors are the eyes of every automated production line.

ROK.robotnik_notes: North American factory automation standard. Connects semiconductor fab equipment with robotic manufacturing systems.

6954 JP.key_suppliers: Servo motor components, rare earth magnets
6954 JP.robotnik_notes: World's largest robot manufacturer (1M+ deployed). $90M Michigan expansion aligns with CHIPS Act reshoring. Rare earth magnet dependency.

RKLB.robotnik_notes: Purest New Space play. Vertically integrated: Electron launch + Space Systems + Neutron in development. Revenue $436M (+55% YoY). Dual revenue model.

ECHO.robotnik_notes: Legacy GEO operator navigating LEO era. Hughes broadband business transitioning.

ASTS.robotnik_notes: Direct-to-cell satellite connectivity. $1.5B+ in MOU commitments. Pre-revenue but creating a new space infrastructure category. Most semiconductor-intensive satellite design.

PL.robotnik_notes: Largest EO constellation (~200 satellites). Daily global imaging. Semiconductor content per satellite rising with onboard AI processing.

KRMN.robotnik_notes: Precision space component consolidator. Roll-up strategy acquiring niche sole-sourced parts suppliers.

3037 TT.robotnik_notes: CoWoS substrate bottleneck — Q1 star (+130.6%). Advanced packaging substrates are the binding constraint on AI chip production. Sole supplier risk.

SQM.robotnik_notes: #2 lithium producer. Atacama brine = lowest-cost lithium source. Battery supply chain for robotics, drones, satellite power.

ALB.robotnik_notes: #1 lithium producer. Geographic diversification (Australia, Chile, US). Battery supply chain for frontier stack mobile systems.

TXN.bottleneck_description: The broadest broad-line analog and embedded supplier, number one in analog at ~18% of a fragmented, competitive field (Analog $14.0bn of $17.7bn CY25 revenue). Frontier exposure (AI-server power, data centre) is diffuse across a very large catalogue and is one of roughly five interchangeable power-IC vendors, with no single-source chokepoint. Competitive field, sourced elsewhere at modest penalty, which is LOW.

IFX GR.bottleneck_description: Global number one in power semiconductors with the fastest-growing AI-server-power line of the analog cohort (over EUR 700m in FY25, guided toward EUR 1.5bn FY26; Automotive ~48% of EUR 14.7bn FY25 revenue). The strongest-position LOW in the set, but power is a genuinely multi-supplier field (STMicro, onsemi, TI, Renesas, MPWR all compete) and AI-power is still a single-digit share of group, so there is no stack-relevant concentration. LOW at the company level; the one to revisit first if AI-power share concentrates.

NXPI.bottleneck_description: Automotive-led broad-line supplier (Automotive 58% of $12.3bn FY25 revenue): radar, vehicle processors, BMS and secure elements. Strong but not sole-source: Infineon, Renesas, STMicro and TI all compete across automotive and MCU, and direct AI-compute exposure is limited. Multi-supplier field with no stack-relevant concentration, which is LOW.

MCHP.bottleneck_description: Broad-line microcontroller and analog supplier (Industrial ~30% of ~$4.4bn FY25 revenue, in a deep cyclical trough), with a small data-centre-connectivity line. Competes across MCU and analog with TI, STMicro, Renesas, NXP and Infineon, with no sole-source frontier position. Competitive multi-supplier field, which is LOW.

ARM.bottleneck_description: Peak position is the Arm instruction-set architecture, on which ~99% of smartphone application-processor designs depend (FY26 20-F; royalty 53% of $4.92bn revenue). Switching the ecosystem to RISC-V or x86 is a multi-year, multi-billion undertaking with no substitute at scale today, which meets the HIGH bar. Not CRITICAL: RISC-V is a viable if immature path, so the position is category-dominant rather than sole-source.

CDNS.bottleneck_description: One of the two firms that hold electronic-design automation, the framework's named HIGH archetype (Cadence plus Synopsys ~61% combined; Core EDA ~70% of $5.30bn FY25 revenue). Tools are qualified over years into foundry-certified sign-off flows, so changing a core tool forces multi-year requalification of the whole design methodology. Category-dominant with deep lock-in, below CRITICAL only because a second vendor exists.

SNPS.bottleneck_description: The other half of the electronic-design-automation duopoly and the framework's named HIGH archetype (number one at ~31%; Design Automation ~75% of $7.05bn FY25 revenue). Same foundry-certified, multi-year tool lock-in as Cadence. Category-dominant, below CRITICAL because Cadence is a qualified alternative.

QCOM.bottleneck_description: Peak position is premium mobile SoCs and modem-RF plus the cellular-SEP licensing book (QCT 87%, QTL 13% of $44.3bn FY25 revenue). The chip business is substitutable at a redesign cost: MediaTek is at premium-Android parity and Apple has designed the Qualcomm modem out toward ~20% of prior volume, eroding its one near-monopoly toward MEDIUM. QTL is a hard-to-avoid royalty moat but not a frontier-stack supply chokepoint, so the company brackets MEDIUM rather than HIGH.

MRVL.bottleneck_description: Peak position is custom AI ASICs, where Marvell is number two in the ~95% Broadcom-Marvell duopoly, plus optical-DSP interconnect leadership, its largest data-centre line (Data Center 74% of $8.19bn FY26 revenue). A hyperscaler substitutes Marvell only through a silicon redesign and requalification cycle, which is the MEDIUM definition, not LOW. Consistency: AVGO, number one in the same duopoly, rates MEDIUM on the same test, so the number two cannot sit a full grade below.

8035 JP.bottleneck_description: Peak position is coater-developer track, where Tokyo Electron holds ~90% global and effectively 100% EUV-layer share of an essential lithography step with no leading-edge alternative (only SCREEN competes, at trailing nodes). Under the peak-position ruling the track franchise's mid-teens revenue share does not lower the grade: the company rates on its most concentrated frontier line, as ASML does on EUV. Category-dominant on an irreplaceable step meets HIGH; below CRITICAL because SCREEN supplies a substitute at lower nodes.

6857 JP.bottleneck_description: Peak position is high-end SoC and HBM/AI-accelerator test, where Advantest leads within the ~80% Advantest-Teradyne ATE duopoly (Test Systems ~90% of JPY 1,128.6bn FY26 revenue). Close call: the duopoly resembles the framework's HIGH EDA archetype, but ATE switching is multi-quarter tester requalification, below the multi-year, multi-billion HIGH bar, so the switching-cost test lands it at MEDIUM. Revisable at review; if the ATE duopoly is judged EDA-equivalent, Advantest moves to HIGH first.

TER.bottleneck_description: Peak position is semiconductor test as co-leader of the ~80% Advantest-Teradyne ATE duopoly (Semi Test 79% of $3.19bn FY25 revenue), blended with a fragmented, competitive robotics arm (Universal Robots ~15% share, 10% of revenue). ATE switching is multi-quarter requalification, below the HIGH bar, and the robotics dilution reinforces MEDIUM. Robust to the ATE-grade question: even if the duopoly were judged HIGH, the fragmented robotics business holds the blend at MEDIUM.

ASX.bottleneck_description: Peak position is outsourced assembly and test, where ASE is the number-one OSAT at ~30% (ATM ~60% of NT$645bn FY25 revenue). A customer can move packaging and test among OSATs (Amkor, JCET, Powertech) at a requalification cost, which is the MEDIUM definition. Guard: ASE is not the advanced-packaging chokepoint; leading-edge CoWoS-class 2.5D sits at TSMC and ASE is a spillover player, so the grade rests on scale-leader qualification friction, not a packaging monopoly.

4063 JP.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is photomask blanks, where Shin-Etsu is number one at about thirty-five per cent but Hoya (about thirty per cent) and AGC are credible alternatives, a three-firm field a mask maker can requalify across at a switching cost. It is also number one in silicon wafers at about thirty per cent within a five-supplier oligopoly. Neither is a category lock: a substitute exists but would need requalification, which is what MEDIUM means. Corrects an earlier rationale that cited a >70% Shin-Etsu/Tosoh ULE-quartz photomask-substrate duopoly; ULE is Corning's EUV-substrate glass and the synthetic-quartz photomask substrate is a three-firm field, so no such duopoly exists.

ADI.bottleneck_description: High-performance analog and mixed-signal supplier, number two in analog at ~13.5% of a fragmented field (top five ~58%; Industrial 45% and Automotive 30% of $11.0bn FY25 revenue). No frontier position is single-sourced and every socket has qualified alternatives, so there is no stack-relevant concentration, which is LOW. Parts are design-in sticky, placing it at the high end of LOW rather than the commodity floor, but the company-level grade is LOW.

MPWR.bottleneck_description: Peak position is power delivery for AI servers and GPU boards, where MPWR was the dominant incumbent on Nvidia's Hopper generation (Enterprise Data plus Storage and Computing ~half of $2.79bn FY25 revenue). LOW because substitution was demonstrated: Nvidia second-sourced Blackwell power to Renesas and Infineon within one architecture generation and MPWR lost share in a boom year, in a competitive five-vendor field. Flip condition: if a future architecture's power requirements narrow the qualified vendor field so switching becomes a board redesign rather than a part swap, the grade moves to MEDIUM; watch the next generation's power-vendor list.

STMPA.bottleneck_description: Broad-line supplier led by automotive (~39% of $11.8bn FY25 revenue): automotive-SiC (with Infineon), MCUs, power and MEMS. Every line is a multi-supplier field (Infineon, onsemi, TI, Renesas, NXP) and AI-compute exposure is indirect. Competitive with no sole-source frontier position, which is LOW.

SYM.bottleneck_description: A warehouse-automation systems integrator whose output is differentiated but replaceable (its 10-K names Dematic, Honeywell, AutoStore, Ocado and Daifuku as competitors; Systems 94% of $2.25bn FY25 revenue). On the supply-substitutability test the frontier stack does not depend on it and a buyer could procure automation from several integrators, which is LOW. Its salient risk is customer concentration (Walmart ~85% of revenue), a commercial exposure on a different axis from supply substitutability, not a bottleneck.

6920 JP.bottleneck_description: Sole commercial supplier of EUV mask blank inspection (MBI) and actinic patterned mask inspection (APMI) tools. EUV reticle manufacturing at advanced nodes cannot be quality-controlled without Lasertec equipment.
6920 JP.key_customers: TSMC, Samsung Foundry, Intel Foundry, mask shops (Toppan, DNP, Hoya, Photronics)
6920 JP.key_suppliers: Carl Zeiss SMT (EUV optics), Japanese subsystem supply chain
6920 JP.robotnik_notes: KLA and Applied Materials do not offer competing EUV-actinic mask inspection. ASML and the foundry/IDM ecosystem publicly acknowledge Lasertec's monopoly in EUV mask inspection. DUV-based mask inspection cannot detect printable defect modes that emerge under EUV exposure at sub-7nm geometries, so the bottleneck deepens as nodes shrink. Mirrors ASML's EUV-scanner monopoly one tier upstream in the mask production chain.

AEIS.bottleneck_description: RF + DC plasma power generators for etch and deposition — structural 3-player market with mid-program switching virtually unheard of.
AEIS.key_customers: Lam Research, Applied Materials, Tokyo Electron
AEIS.robotnik_notes: Plasma power is structurally a 3-player oligopoly (AEIS, MKS-ENI, Comet). Customers (etch/deposition OEMs) qualify multiple suppliers but switching mid-program is rare due to qualification complexity. Revised from MEDIUM after consideration of mid-program switching friction in advanced-node fab build-outs.

FORM.bottleneck_description: Wafer probe cards — dominant in HBM probe-card segment; the AI-memory ramp leverages this position as the highest-value subsegment of test infrastructure.
FORM.key_customers: Micron, SK Hynix, Samsung (HBM test); leading-edge logic test customers
FORM.robotnik_notes: Probe cards are a 3-supplier market (FormFactor, MJC, Technoprobe). FormFactor's HBM probe-card position is leveraged by the AI-memory ramp — HBM cards have multi-quarter qualification timelines, making mid-program switching impractical. Revised from MEDIUM given the HBM-specific dominance in the highest-value test segment.

KLIC.bottleneck_description: Wire bonders + ball bonders for IC packaging — effectively a duopoly with ASMPT for advanced wire-bonding, the mainstream IC packaging interconnect.
KLIC.key_customers: OSATs (Amkor, ASE, JCET), IDM packaging operations
KLIC.robotnik_notes: Advanced wire-bonding is a 2-player market (KLIC + ASMPT). Wire-bond capacity remains structurally relevant even as advanced packaging grows — high pin-count BGAs and power devices continue to require wire bonders. Switching cost is multi-quarter (qualification of bond profiles for each device family). Revised from MEDIUM on the structural duopoly basis.

TSEM.bottleneck_description: Specialty foundry — RF SOI, high-voltage analog, BCD, SiGe. RF SOI capacity in particular is mission-critical for smartphone PA chips with multi-year qualification cycles.
TSEM.key_customers: RF chip designers (Qorvo, Skyworks, Broadcom), power management ICs
TSEM.robotnik_notes: RF SOI capacity is structurally tight — Tower + GlobalFoundries are the merchant suppliers for smartphone PA chips. Failed Intel acquisition (2022-23) demonstrated the strategic value of this capacity. Multi-year process qualification creates real switching friction for fabless customers. Revised from MEDIUM on merchant-supplier oligopoly grounds.

ALAB.bottleneck_description: Leading PCIe Gen5/6 retimers + CXL interconnect for AI server fabric — niche leader with TSMC fab dependence.
ALAB.key_customers: Hyperscalers (Meta, MS, AWS), AI server OEMs
ALAB.robotnik_notes: Hyperscalers are dual-sourcing across Astera/Marvell/Credo. TSMC dependence on the fab side adds an upstream constraint. Switching cost is real (board-level qualification) but substitutes exist.

ALGM.bottleneck_description: Magnetic sensors + power for automotive — auto qualification creates real switching friction, especially in safety-rated Hall-effect positions.
ALGM.robotnik_notes: Hall-effect sensors compete with Melexis, Infineon, NXP, TI; the auto-qualification process (AEC-Q100, ISO 26262) makes mid-platform switching multi-year. Revised from LOW given the auto-qualification dynamic.

AMKR.bottleneck_description: Largest US-based OSAT (outsourced assembly + test) — strategic position in CHIPS Act packaging-incentive build-out.
AMKR.key_customers: Semiconductor IDMs, fabless customers, US government contracts
AMKR.robotnik_notes: Global OSAT is a 3-4 player market (ASE ~30%, Amkor ~15%, JCET, Powertech). CHIPS Act packaging incentives add US-specific bargaining position.

CAMT.bottleneck_description: Israeli advanced-packaging inspection — bumps, RDL, copper pillars. Position strengthens with CoWoS / hybrid-bonding build-out.
CAMT.key_customers: OSATs and IDMs running advanced packaging lines
CAMT.robotnik_notes: Direct competition with Onto Innovation; KLA upstream. Advanced-packaging ramp (CoWoS, hybrid bonding) strengthens position.

CRDO.bottleneck_description: Active Electrical Cables (AECs) + serdes for AI cluster interconnect — niche leader competing for hyperscaler sockets.
CRDO.robotnik_notes: Direct competition with Marvell, Astera Labs, MACOM. Niche leader but customers have substitution paths.

LASR.bottleneck_description: High-power fibre lasers + photonic ICs for industrial + defence (directed-energy programs).
LASR.key_customers: DoD (HELSI, OPIR), industrial laser systems integrators
LASR.robotnik_notes: Defence procurement creates qualified-part-list switching friction. Coherent (COHR), IPG Photonics, Trumpf compete in commercial high-power laser.

LSCC.bottleneck_description: Low-power FPGA leader at sub-65nm process nodes — owns the low-density low-power FPGA niche.
LSCC.key_customers: Industrial, comms, AI inference at edge
LSCC.robotnik_notes: AMD (Xilinx) competes upmarket; Microchip in adjacencies. Toolchain lock-in slows but doesn't block substitution.

MKSI.bottleneck_description: Vacuum gauges, gas delivery, motion control, photonics subsystems for fab tools — largest pure-play fab subsystem supplier.
MKSI.key_customers: Wafer-fab equipment OEMs (Lam, AMAT, Tokyo Electron, ASML)
MKSI.robotnik_notes: Many products are mission-critical (vacuum interfaces specifically), but per-segment competitors exist (Brooks, Edwards, Watlow). Atotech acquisition adds chemistry/plating exposure.

MTSI.bottleneck_description: RF + photonic ICs for telco/datacenter optical + defence. Acquired Wolfspeed RF business 2024.
MTSI.key_customers: Telco infrastructure OEMs, datacenter optical module makers, defence contractors
MTSI.robotnik_notes: Defence-relevant content increases switching friction (qualified-part lists). Qorvo, Skyworks, Sumitomo Electric, Broadcom all compete in commercial RF.

NVMI.robotnik_notes: KLA is structurally larger; Onto Innovation is the closest peer. Nova owns OCD metrology niche for several process-control loops; substitutes exist but require recalibration.

NVTS.bottleneck_description: GaN power ICs for fast chargers and (emerging) EV/datacenter.
NVTS.key_customers: Charger/adapter ODMs, EV power electronics OEMs
NVTS.robotnik_notes: Leader in fast-charger GaN, but GaN itself is an emerging power-device category with multiple suppliers (Infineon's GaN Systems acquisition, Power Integrations, EPC, Transphorm, STMicro). SiC remains a substitute at higher voltages.

ONTO.bottleneck_description: Macro defect inspection + lithography metrology + advanced-packaging inspection.
ONTO.robotnik_notes: KLA dominates patterned-wafer inspection; Onto leads in macro inspection and advanced-packaging metrology. Substitutes per-application but not blanket.

PI.bottleneck_description: RAIN RFID readers + IC tags — structural duopoly with NXP. Reader infrastructure ties to IC encoding at scale.
PI.robotnik_notes: RAIN UHF passive RFID IC market is a long-running duopoly with NXP. Reader infrastructure (encoding, antennas) is tied to ICs, so single-supplier defection at scale is multi-year. Structural duopoly persists even with one named substitute.

PLAB.bottleneck_description: Merchant photomask supplier in a structurally concentrated market.
PLAB.key_customers: Foundries, IDMs without captive mask shops
PLAB.robotnik_notes: Structurally concentrated market (Photronics + DNP + Toppan + Hoya). Captive mask shops at Samsung/Intel/SMIC reduce merchant TAM but provide no substitution for non-IDM customers.

RMBS.bottleneck_description: Memory interface IP (DDR5 RDIMM, CXL.mem) + security IP.
RMBS.key_customers: Memory controllers (AMD, Intel), CXL ecosystem participants
RMBS.robotnik_notes: Owns several memory-interface patents that are difficult to design around for DDR5/CXL. Synopsys and Cadence offer competing IP for adjacent functions; Rambus's RCD/MRDIMM positioning gives near-term dominance with CXL substitution paths emerging.

SITM.bottleneck_description: MEMS-based silicon clocks/oscillators displacing legacy quartz.
SITM.robotnik_notes: Dominant in MEMS oscillators (~90% share). Quartz-based suppliers (Epson, NDK, Kyocera) remain technically substitutable in most designs, but the timing-precision advantage of MEMS creates lock-in once specified.

SKYT.bottleneck_description: US trusted-foundry (DoD STA-2 approved) for defence + emerging-customer R&D.
SKYT.key_customers: DoD programs, R&D startups requiring trusted-foundry status
SKYT.robotnik_notes: Narrow customer base. GlobalFoundries also holds trusted-foundry credentials; Intel Foundry Services emerging. SkyWater's niche is small but defensible for strategic-supply programs.

SMTC.bottleneck_description: LoRa wireless platform near-monopoly + analog mixed-signal.
SMTC.key_customers: LPWAN network operators, IoT device OEMs, broadband infrastructure
SMTC.robotnik_notes: LoRa owns LPWAN niche, but cellular IoT (NB-IoT, LTE-M) is a credible substitute architecture chosen by carriers globally. Switching cost is moderate (firmware redesign).

WOLF.bottleneck_description: Largest US-based 200mm SiC substrate + SiC MOSFET capacity (Mohawk Valley fab).
WOLF.key_customers: EV power electronics OEMs, industrial inverter makers, defence
WOLF.robotnik_notes: US national-security-relevant SiC substrate position (CHIPS Act funded), but global SiC market has credible substitutes (Coherent's 200mm rollout, ROHM, Sumitomo, Infineon vertical). Going-concern risk is real (Ch.11 watch as of late 2025) — flagged separately rather than weighted into the structural bottleneck rating.
WOLF.going_concern_note: Chapter 11 watch as of late 2025; structural bottleneck rating reflects the asset position not the corporate solvency.

AMBA.bottleneck_description: Video processing SoCs for automotive ADAS + security cameras.
AMBA.robotnik_notes: Competitive market: NVIDIA (Drive), Mobileye, Qualcomm Snapdragon Auto, Sony semiconductor substitute.

AOSL.robotnik_notes: Infineon, ON Semi, ST, TI, Nexperia substitute in mainstream power discretes.

CEVA.bottleneck_description: Licensed DSP IP for audio + Bluetooth + computer vision.
CEVA.key_customers: Mobile SoC vendors, IoT silicon vendors
CEVA.robotnik_notes: Arm, Synopsys ARC, Cadence Tensilica substitute. In-house cores at hyperscalers.

CRUS.robotnik_notes: Realtek, NXP, Knowles substitute in audio codec niches.

INDI.bottleneck_description: Auto sensor interface + mmWave radar (subscale vs. peers).
INDI.robotnik_notes: Subscale vs NXP, ST, TI, Renesas, Bosch in auto radar and sensor interface markets.

MELE.robotnik_notes: Allegro (also in this batch, MEDIUM), Infineon, NXP, TI substitute. Note: Melexis is positioned closer to commodity Hall-effect than the safety-rated Allegro positions that justified MEDIUM there; this is a deliberate rating differentiation within the same product family.

MXL.robotnik_notes: Broadcom, Marvell, MediaTek compete by segment.

NVEC.robotnik_notes: TDK, Allegro, Honeywell substitute. Public bottleneck data is thin given the small mcap and narrow product family — confidence flagged.

ON.robotnik_notes: SiC + CMOS image sensors are both competitive markets. SiC competes with Wolfspeed/Infineon/STMicro; CMOS image sensors compete with Sony, Samsung.

POWI.bottleneck_description: Offline switcher ICs for AC-DC power conversion.
POWI.key_customers: Consumer electronics OEMs, industrial power supply makers
POWI.robotnik_notes: Navitas (GaN), TI, Infineon, STMicro substitute in offline switcher and AC-DC niches.

QRVO.bottleneck_description: RFFE peer of Skyworks — same customer concentration, same substitution paths.
QRVO.robotnik_notes: Apple dual-sources RFFE with Skyworks, Broadcom, Murata. Highly competitive.

SLAB.bottleneck_description: IoT MCU + multi-protocol wireless (Bluetooth, Zigbee, Z-Wave, Matter).
SLAB.robotnik_notes: Highly competitive (NXP, Nordic, ST, TI, Espressif).

SWKS.bottleneck_description: RFFE for handset/IoT. Apple ~50% of revenue, but dual-sourced.
SWKS.robotnik_notes: RFFE for handset/IoT. Apple dual-sources with Qorvo + Broadcom + Murata.

SYNA.robotnik_notes: Goodix, FocalTech, MediaTek substitute across touch and IoT comms.

UMC.key_customers: Fabless customers in legacy and mature nodes
UMC.robotnik_notes: Mature-node pure-play foundry is competitive — GlobalFoundries, SMIC, Vanguard, Tower substitute.

002050.bottleneck_description: Qualified Tesla supplier for EV thermal management valves, expansion valves, and electronic pumps; designated for Tesla Optimus actuator joints.
002050.key_customers: Tesla, BYD, Volkswagen, Geely, Daikin, Midea, Gree
002050.key_suppliers: Steel/brass alloy mills, rare earth magnet suppliers (CNRE downstream)
002050.robotnik_notes: Sanhua is a leading global supplier of HVAC/refrigeration valves and a designated Tesla Tier-1 for NEV thermal management (~RMB 1,300/vehicle in Model 3). Switching costs are real in EV TMS where Sanhua has multi-year qualification with major OEMs, and the Tesla Optimus actuator partnership adds humanoid optionality. However, alternatives exist (Danfoss, DunAn, Saginomiya) in refrigeration valves, so this is qualification-friction MEDIUM rather than monopoly HIGH.

300124 C2.bottleneck_description: Dominant China servo drive + low-voltage VFD supplier with ~40% domestic servo share; deep penetration into robot joint motors and industrial automation.
300124 C2.key_customers: Chinese industrial robot OEMs, EV battery equipment makers, CNC builders, humanoid robot startups
300124 C2.key_suppliers: Power semiconductor suppliers (STM, Infineon), rare earth magnet suppliers, MCU vendors
300124 C2.robotnik_notes: Inovance is the largest industrial automation player in China with leading shares in general-purpose servo systems and VFDs, and supplies servo motors for ~70% of domestic robot joint applications. While Inovance dominates China, global servo competition (Yaskawa, Mitsubishi, Siemens, Rockwell, ABB) is strong and switching is feasible outside China, so MEDIUM reflects China-only qualification stickiness rather than global monopoly.

6273 JP.bottleneck_description: Global #1 pneumatic automation supplier (~30% global share) of solenoid valves, cylinders, and air treatment equipment for factory automation.
6273 JP.key_customers: TSMC, Samsung, semiconductor fab equipment makers (AMAT, ASML), automotive OEMs, packaging machine builders
6273 JP.key_suppliers: Aluminum/steel suppliers, valve coil and electronics suppliers
6273 JP.robotnik_notes: SMC is the clear global leader in pneumatic components with ~30% share, ahead of Festo, Parker-Hannifin, Airtac, and CKD. Pneumatic valves are qualified into specific automation lines (semi front-end tools, packaging, automotive assembly) where re-qualification takes months, supporting MEDIUM. Below HIGH because the pneumatic technology stack itself has many capable players globally, and pneumatics is partially substitutable by electric actuators.

601100.bottleneck_description: World's largest excavator hydraulic cylinder supplier (~30% global share) with growing presence in hydraulic pumps, motors, and valves for construction machinery.
601100.key_customers: Sany, XCMG, Zoomlion, Caterpillar (limited), Komatsu (limited), Volvo CE
601100.key_suppliers: Steel/alloy mills, sealing technology suppliers, casting foundries
601100.robotnik_notes: Hengli broke the Japanese-European duopoly (Kawasaki, Bosch Rexroth, Eaton) in excavator hydraulic cylinders and now serves all major Chinese OEMs (Sany, XCMG, Zoomlion) and key international names. Switching cylinders requires re-engineering for fit/pressure ratings, creating real friction. MEDIUM reflects Hengli's structural cost advantage in cylinders + entrenchment in China construction, but with viable global substitutes (Kawasaki, Bosch Rexroth) the bottleneck is not HIGH.

688017.bottleneck_description: China's largest harmonic reducer manufacturer with ~26-40% domestic share; primary domestic alternative to Harmonic Drive Systems Japan for robot wrist joints.
688017.key_customers: Estun, Siasun, Unitree, UBTech, Xiaomi, EFORT, Chinese cobot makers
688017.key_suppliers: Specialty steel mills, precision grinding equipment suppliers, bearing suppliers
688017.robotnik_notes: Leaderdrive (Leader Harmonious) is the de-facto Chinese substitute for Harmonic Drive Japan in small-joint robot reducers, increasingly qualified into humanoid robot programs (Unitree, UBTech, Xiaomi). It now meets a meaningful chunk of China robot demand at materially lower cost. MEDIUM reflects rapidly growing qualification with Chinese humanoid programs and structural cost advantage versus 6324 JP, but well below HIGH because alternatives (HD Systems, Sumitomo, ShuangHuan reducers, Lifeng) exist.

1590 TT.bottleneck_description: #2 pneumatic component supplier in China (~30% share) producing cylinders, valves, and FRLs; positioned as cost-disruptive alternative to SMC/Festo.
1590 TT.key_customers: Chinese automation system integrators, EV battery makers (CATL), packaging machine OEMs, semiconductor tool builders
1590 TT.key_suppliers: Aluminum extrusion mills, solenoid coil suppliers, seal/elastomer suppliers
1590 TT.robotnik_notes: Airtac has gained share aggressively from Japanese pneumatics incumbents on price and now holds ~30% of China pneumatics, with plans to reach 33-35% by 2028-2030. However, the pneumatic component market is structurally competitive with SMC, Festo, Parker, CKD, and various Chinese players (Yadeke, etc.). Airtac is a strong margin operator but its product line is broadly substitutable, supporting LOW.

002472.bottleneck_description: Leading China automotive gear specialist (passenger vehicle, commercial vehicle, construction machinery) with growing RV reducer presence for industrial robots.
002472.key_customers: Chinese auto OEMs (BYD, Geely, Chery), construction machinery makers (Sany), industrial robot makers
002472.key_suppliers: Forging steel mills, heat-treatment service providers, gear-grinding equipment suppliers
002472.robotnik_notes: Shuanghuan is the leading domestic gear maker and was an early Chinese entrant in RV reducers, but its robotics RV reducer business is still small versus Nabtesco globally, and its core automotive gear business is broadly competitive. Several Chinese gear makers (Qinchuan, Zhongda Leader) compete in similar segments. LOW reflects peer-competitive positioning despite scale advantage.

6481 JP.bottleneck_description: World #1 linear motion (LM) guide and ball screw supplier; precision class deeply qualified into semiconductor lithography, machine tool, and high-precision robotics.
6481 JP.key_customers: ASML, Nikon, Tokyo Electron, Yaskawa, FANUC, semiconductor fab equipment makers, machine tool builders
6481 JP.key_suppliers: Bearing steel suppliers, precision grinding service providers, ceramic component suppliers
6481 JP.robotnik_notes: THK invented the linear motion guide in 1972 and remains global #1 in precision linear guides, with deep qualification into ASML/Nikon lithography, Yaskawa robots, and precision machine tools. While Hiwin, NSK, Bosch Rexroth, Schaeffler, and IKO contest the broader market, THK retains premium-class incumbency in high-precision/semi-grade applications. MEDIUM reflects this qualification stickiness in critical applications while acknowledging viable substitutes exist outside the precision tier.

2049.bottleneck_description: World #3 in ball screws and major supplier of linear guideways; growing position in industrial robots and semiconductor-grade precision motion components.
2049.key_customers: Machine tool builders, semiconductor equipment OEMs, EV battery equipment makers, Taiwanese/Chinese cobot makers
2049.key_suppliers: Bearing steel mills, precision grinding equipment, motor and drive suppliers
2049.robotnik_notes: Hiwin is the leading Taiwanese motion components maker and a peer-competitor to THK and Bosch Rexroth in ball screws and linear guides. It has structural cost advantage versus Japanese incumbents while still meeting precision requirements for many semiconductor and industrial automation applications, with qualification into machine tool and EV battery equipment lines. MEDIUM reflects real qualification stickiness for precision-grade screws/guides while noting the segment has multiple credible suppliers.

6324.bottleneck_description: Inventor and dominant supplier of strain-wave (harmonic) gears used in robot wrist/elbow joints and humanoid-robot dexterous joints; standard-class incumbent across global cobot/industrial robot designs.
6324.key_customers: FANUC, Yaskawa, Universal Robots, ABB, Tesla, Figure AI, Apptronik, satellite/space programs
6324.key_suppliers: Bearing steel mills, precision grinding/honing equipment suppliers, gear-cutting tool suppliers
6324.robotnik_notes: Harmonic Drive Systems holds dominant share in high-precision strain-wave gears - the standard small-joint reducer in cobots (UR, FANUC CRX), industrial robot wrists, and humanoid robot designs (Tesla Optimus, Figure 02, Apptronik). Switching to alternatives (Sumitomo, Leaderdrive) requires gear-class re-qualification and the precision class remains the gold standard. HIGH (not CRITICAL) because Chinese alternatives (Leaderdrive especially) have been validated for cost-sensitive applications and the moat is eroding, but global premium share remains highly concentrated. Adversarial verifier flagged dual-sourcing already underway: Suzhou Green Harmonic (688017) now primary Tesla Optimus harmonic-reducer supplier at 30-40% discount, Leaderdrive humanoid revenue grew from negligible to 30% of Q1 2025 revenue, Jefferies downgraded to Underperform. Original HIGH proposal downgraded to MEDIUM by user-approved verifier verdict.

6268 JP.bottleneck_description: Dominant global supplier of RV (cycloidal) reducers used in the base, shoulder, and elbow joints of articulated industrial robots; ~35-60% global share in robot RV reducers.
6268 JP.key_customers: FANUC, Yaskawa, ABB, KUKA, Kawasaki, Mitsubishi Electric, humanoid robot OEMs, Boeing/Airbus (aerospace actuators), railway brake market
6268 JP.key_suppliers: Specialty bearing steel suppliers, precision grinding equipment, casting foundries
6268 JP.robotnik_notes: Nabtesco RV reducers and Harmonic Drive strain-wave gears together form the de-facto duopoly enabling global industrial robot production. Nabtesco holds 35-60% share in RV reducers with top-3 (Nabtesco/Sumitomo/Spinea) collectively above 80%. RV reducer qualification at robot OEMs spans multi-year validation cycles and the precision class remains hard to match. HIGH (not CRITICAL) reflects credible alternatives (Sumitomo, Spinea, emerging Chinese suppliers like Shuanghuan) but with prohibitive switching cost in premium robot platforms.

600111.bottleneck_description: Sole dominant global producer of separated NdPr oxide from the Bayan Obo deposit; controls ~90% of refined rare-earth magnet feedstock at the production-quota level, with no viable Western alternative at scale.
600111.key_customers: NdFeB magnet makers (JL Mag, Ningbo Yunsheng, Zhongke Sanhuan, Proterial/Hitachi Metals); downstream EV motor, robotics, wind turbine, and defense supply chains
600111.key_suppliers: Baogang Group (parent — Bayan Obo mining), separation chemical suppliers, Chinese state coordination on export quotas
600111.robotnik_notes: CNRE controls the Bayan Obo complex (world's largest light rare earth resource) and is the dominant single producer of separated NdPr oxide globally. China collectively refines ~90% of global rare earth magnet inputs and CNRE is the largest single operator — its production quotas materially move global NdPr prices within weeks. The 2024 and 2025 Chinese rare-earth export controls (October 2024 Annex IV additions; April/October 2025 expansions covering medium and heavy REEs) have escalated geopolitical bite from 'concentration risk' to 'active supply-chain weaponisation' — clearing the CRITICAL bar of 'no alternative exists today'. MP Materials (Mountain Pass), Lynas, and emerging Western processing capacity (Arafura, etc.) collectively run at <15% of CNRE's separation throughput and lack heavy-rare-earth processing capability outside Lynas's Kalgoorlie ramp. Consolidated key (was split as '600111' HIGH from Robotics batch + '600111 C1' CRITICAL from existing rated set; the existing CRITICAL was the right call given full context).

002008 C2.bottleneck_description: Largest Chinese industrial laser equipment maker (cutting, marking, PCB drilling) competing with Raycus, MaxPhotonics, IPG and TRUMPF.
002008 C2.key_customers: Chinese EV/battery makers, PCB fabs, consumer-electronics assembly lines
002008 C2.key_suppliers: Domestic laser-source vendors (Raycus, MaxPhotonics) plus optics importers
002008 C2.robotnik_notes: Han's is the volume leader in China across laser marking/cutting machines (claimed >70% domestic share in marking historically and #1 in metal cutting today), but the underlying tech is contested with multiple Chinese and foreign substitutes. Customers can switch suppliers within a single procurement cycle, and most segments are commoditizing. Genuine bottleneck status would require a unique capability, which is absent.

LECO.bottleneck_description: Largest North American welding equipment/consumables supplier; competes head-to-head with ITW/Miller, ESAB, Kemppi.
LECO.key_customers: Heavy industry, construction, shipyards, automotive welding cells, energy
LECO.key_suppliers: Steel/wire raw materials, electronics for inverters
LECO.robotnik_notes: Lincoln has ~18% global welding share and strong brand, but the welding equipment and consumables market is structurally competitive with multiple credible alternatives (ITW/Miller, ESAB, Fronius, Panasonic, Daihen). Switching is operationally easy; consumables interchange across vendors. No sole-source choke-point.

2395 TT.bottleneck_description: Industrial PC and embedded-board leader (~34-40% share) with high qualification stickiness in long-life industrial deployments.
2395 TT.key_customers: Factory automation OEMs, medical equipment, transportation, energy, retail kiosks, NVIDIA-certified edge AI partners
2395 TT.key_suppliers: Intel/AMD CPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, memory/storage vendors
2395 TT.robotnik_notes: Advantech holds 34-40% of global industrial PC share -- the largest single share in the segment -- and its products are designed-into long-lifecycle industrial systems with multi-year qualification cycles. Switching to Kontron, Beckhoff, Siemens or Asus IPC adds engineering revalidation cost. However, viable substitutes do exist with peer technical capability, so the position is MEDIUM not HIGH.

6506 JP.bottleneck_description: Big-4 industrial robot manufacturer with strong servo motor/motion control franchise; peer-competitive with Fanuc, ABB, KUKA.
6506 JP.key_customers: Automotive OEMs (welding, painting), electronics assembly, semiconductor handling, general industrial
6506 JP.key_suppliers: Renesas, Rohm and other Japanese semiconductor and component suppliers
6506 JP.robotnik_notes: Yaskawa is a Big-4 robot OEM (~8-12% share) and a leader in servo motors and AC drives, but the Big-4 oligopoly is contested both internally and increasingly by Chinese entrants (Estun, Inovance, Siasun) plus collaborative-robot challengers. Calibration anchor 6954 JP Fanuc is LOW; Yaskawa sits in the same peer set. Servo motors are also a competitive subsystem with Mitsubishi, Siemens, Rockwell and Chinese alternatives.

KCR FH.bottleneck_description: Industrial overhead crane and port-equipment maker; #3-4 European share, competes with Liebherr, Terex, Cargotec, ZPMC.
KCR FH.key_customers: Steel mills, ports, automotive plants, paper mills, warehouse/logistics customers
KCR FH.key_suppliers: Steel structures, motors, drives, control electronics vendors
KCR FH.robotnik_notes: Konecranes is a credible global player but holds only ~15-20% of European industrial crane share with substantial competition from Liebherr (~35% EU share), Terex/Demag, and Chinese players (XCMG, Zoomlion, ZPMC). Crane procurement is cross-shoppable and substitutable.

6645 JP.bottleneck_description: Broad factory automation portfolio (PLC, sensors, switches, vision); peer-competitive vs Siemens, Rockwell, Mitsubishi, Keyence.
6645 JP.key_customers: Global discrete-manufacturing factories across automotive, electronics, packaging
6645 JP.robotnik_notes: Omron is a competent mid-tier FA vendor (~5-7% in its sub-segments) but faces a strong oligopoly above it (Siemens >20% PLC share, Rockwell 19% in NA, Mitsubishi, Schneider) and below it in sensors from Keyence. Switching from Omron to a competitor is operationally feasible within a project cycle. No bottleneck position.

6113 JP.bottleneck_description: Top-3 global machine tool/sheet-metal fabrication vendor; competes with TRUMPF, Bystronic, Mazak, Mitsubishi, Chinese entrants.
6113 JP.key_customers: Mid-market metal fabricators, auto and aerospace component shops
6113 JP.key_suppliers: Laser sources (IPG, TRUMPF, nLIGHT), CNC controllers, hydraulic/electric drives
6113 JP.robotnik_notes: Amada is a top-3 machine tool franchise (~9.5% share) with strong brand and customer captivity in mid-market fabricators, but the segment has multiple credible substitutes (TRUMPF #1, Bystronic, Mitsubishi, Salvagnini, Trumpf-owned brands) plus increasing Chinese low-cost entries. Switching costs are real but bounded; no sole-source position.

6845 JP.bottleneck_description: Process automation/instrumentation and building automation; mid-tier global player competing with ABB, Emerson, Honeywell, Yokogawa.
6845 JP.robotnik_notes: Azbil holds a respected niche in process control and building automation but faces a deep competitive set (ABB, Emerson, Honeywell, Yokogawa, Siemens, Schneider). Its products are substitutable within typical project lifecycles; no documented sole-source position.

IPGP.bottleneck_description: Global leader in high-power fiber lasers with vertical integration in pump diodes; structural top-5 oligopoly with TRUMPF, Coherent, nLIGHT, Lumentum.
IPGP.key_customers: EV battery weld lines, cutting/welding integrators (Amada, Bystronic, Han's), aerospace, defense directed energy
IPGP.key_suppliers: Internally vertically integrated in pump diodes; specialty optics from Lumentum/Coherent peers
IPGP.robotnik_notes: IPG has structural leadership in high-power industrial fiber lasers with vertical integration in pump diodes (a real moat that took peers ~15 years to approach). The top-5 cohort controls >60% of fiber laser share, and IPG remains the de-facto reference for >10kW industrial cutting/welding. However, Chinese Raycus (~30% China share) and MaxPhotonics have eroded the moat in commodity power bands, and Coherent/TRUMPF compete at the high end. MEDIUM reflects oligopoly position with credible substitutes at most power tiers.

6134 JP.bottleneck_description: Top-3 SMT placement-equipment vendor (with ASMPT and Yamaha) -- structural oligopoly in chip-mounter machines.
6134 JP.key_customers: Global EMS (Foxconn, Pegatron, Flex), OEMs running in-house PCB assembly, automotive electronics suppliers
6134 JP.key_suppliers: Linear motion components, vision systems, custom electronics
6134 JP.robotnik_notes: SMT placement is a structural 3-player oligopoly (Fuji + ASMPT + Yamaha) with high process-engineering know-how and qualified-recipe stickiness across customer factories. Cross-vendor switching requires nozzle library, vision recipe and feeder reconfiguration that takes quarters. Not a sole-source (each competitor offers full-range substitutes), justifying MEDIUM rather than HIGH.

002747 C2.bottleneck_description: Largest domestic Chinese industrial-robot brand (~10% China share) plus vertically integrated servo/controller stack.
002747 C2.key_customers: Chinese photovoltaic, lithium battery, 3C electronics, welding integrators
002747 C2.key_suppliers: Internally integrated servo/controller; reducer imports (Nabtesco, Harmonic) historically
002747 C2.robotnik_notes: Estun ranks #1 among Chinese robot brands at ~10.5% domestic share, but the China industrial-robot market is competitive (Inovance, Siasun, Efort) and global incumbents (Fanuc, Yaskawa, ABB, KUKA) still hold roughly 45% of Chinese share. Estun's customers can substitute robots within months. Vertical-integration is a margin advantage, not a bottleneck.

300024 C2.bottleneck_description: Chinese Academy of Sciences-spin-off integrator (~6% China share) across industrial, mobile, and cobot lines.
300024 C2.key_customers: Chinese discrete-manufacturing customers, AGV/AMR deployments for warehousing
300024 C2.key_suppliers: Domestic motors/drives plus imported reducers and controllers
300024 C2.robotnik_notes: Siasun is a top-5 Chinese robot vendor (~6.2% domestic share) with strong policy ties but trails Estun and Inovance, and broadly competes against Big-4 incumbents in China. Customers have full substitution paths. No bottleneck position.

ATS CN.bottleneck_description: Custom automation systems integrator (life sciences, food, EV battery, transportation); peer-competitive with JR Automation, Hahn, Krones, Scott Automation.
ATS CN.key_customers: Pharma/medical device manufacturers, EV battery cell makers, consumer-goods packaging
ATS CN.key_suppliers: Fanuc/ABB/Kuka robot arms, Siemens/Rockwell PLCs, vision systems
ATS CN.robotnik_notes: ATS sells project-bespoke automation lines into competitive procurement processes. Multiple alternatives exist (JR Automation, Hahn, Festo, Comau, Scott, ABB Engineering) with similar capabilities. No sole-source or oligopoly position; differentiation is primarily execution and customer relationships.

6141 JP.bottleneck_description: Top-2 global CNC machining-center vendor (with Yamazaki Mazak); competes with Okuma, Makino, Haas, JTEKT, DN Solutions.
6141 JP.key_customers: Aerospace, automotive, medical device, mold-and-die shops worldwide
6141 JP.robotnik_notes: Top-4 (TRUMPF, DMG Mori, Mazak, Amada) together hold only ~42% of global metal-fabrication revenue, indicating a fragmented market with viable substitutes at every tier. CNC machining centers are routinely cross-shopped; switching requires retraining but not multi-year qualification. No bottleneck.

6622 JP.bottleneck_description: OTC Daihen is a leading arc-welding robot brand with strong Japanese auto OEM footprint; competes with Yaskawa, Panasonic, Fanuc, Nachi, Kuka in welding cells.
6622 JP.key_customers: Japanese auto OEMs, transformer/grid customers, semiconductor (RF generators)
6622 JP.robotnik_notes: Daihen's OTC welding robot franchise claims global leadership in arc-welding robots, but the segment is highly contested by Yaskawa Motoman, Panasonic, Fanuc and ABB. Welding cell procurement is competitive. Daihen also makes semiconductor RF generators where AEIS dominates -- it is not the marginal supplier. No bottleneck.

688165 C1.bottleneck_description: Top-5 Chinese industrial robot brand; concentration in PV/3C/auto integration with cross-shop substitutes.
688165 C1.key_customers: Chinese solar cell makers (55% of robot revenue), 3C electronics, auto Tier-1 customers; overseas OEMs (Stellantis, GM, VW, Toyota for niche projects)
688165 C1.key_suppliers: Italian acquisitions (CMA paint robots, EVOLUT integrator, ROBOX motion-control)
688165 C1.robotnik_notes: EFORT is a designated Chinese 'little giant' in robotics but is a smaller share than Estun/Inovance/Siasun domestically and competes head-on with Big-4 in China and globally. Robot procurement is substitutable across vendors within a project cycle. No bottleneck position.

6104 JP.bottleneck_description: Mid-tier injection-molding and machine-tool maker (ex-Toshiba Machine); competes with Sumitomo Heavy, JSW, ENGEL, KraussMaffei, Sodick.
6104 JP.key_customers: Automotive component molders, electronics moulders, die-casters
6104 JP.robotnik_notes: Shibaura holds an estimated 15-20% share in high-end large electric injection molding machines but faces credible substitutes from Sumitomo, JSW, ENGEL, KraussMaffei and Chinese low-cost entrants. Customers cross-shop molding machines across procurement cycles. No sole-source position.

6258 JP.bottleneck_description: Custom factory-automation integrator for autos, semiconductors and appliances; 'factory that builds factories' model.
6258 JP.key_customers: Japanese auto OEMs, semiconductor fabs (wafer-handling EFEM/load ports/wafer transfer robots), appliance manufacturers
6258 JP.key_suppliers: Robot arms (Fanuc, Yaskawa), motors, vision systems
6258 JP.robotnik_notes: Hirata is a respected systems integrator with niche capability in semiconductor wafer-handling EFEMs (competes with Brooks Automation, RORZE, Sinfonia, DAIHEN, Yaskawa). Sub-segments are competitive with multiple qualified vendors. No sole-source position justifying a higher rating.

090360 KS.bottleneck_description: LG Electronics' captive robotics supplier (cartesian, SCARA, parallel, glass-transfer); display/electronics handling focus.
090360 KS.key_suppliers: Korean motor/drive vendors plus imported components
090360 KS.robotnik_notes: Robostar operates primarily as a captive supplier to LG Electronics with revenue stability but no external supply-chain bottleneck. Competitors in display/electronics handling robots include Yaskawa, Fanuc, Hirata, DAIHEN, RORZE -- all substitutable. Captive relationship is not a bottleneck position for the broader market.

CGNX.bottleneck_description: Machine vision systems (~11-21% share) sharing the global machine vision market with Keyence, Basler, Teledyne, Omron and SICK in a 5-player 20-30% fragmented oligopoly.
CGNX.key_customers: Amazon (logistics), automotive OEMs, EV battery manufacturers, consumer electronics assemblers, semiconductor packaging
CGNX.key_suppliers: Sony (CMOS image sensors), FPGA/ASIC vendors, optical lens manufacturers
CGNX.robotnik_notes: Cognex is a top-2 global machine vision player alongside Keyence, with deep learning (VisionPro/In-Sight) and developer ecosystem providing stickiness. However the market is contested by Keyence, Basler, Teledyne DALSA, Omron, SICK and MVTec; logistics and automotive customers (52% of revenue) routinely run multi-vendor vision stacks. Software moat creates switching friction but realistic substitution paths exist at the application level; rating aligns with LOW anchor for contested industrial automation incumbents.

NOVT.bottleneck_description: Precision photonics, optical encoders, motors and servo drives designed-in to medical, surgical-robot and advanced-industrial OEM platforms with long regulatory/qualification cycles.
NOVT.key_customers: Medical device OEMs (Stryker-style surgical robots), industrial laser system makers, semiconductor capital equipment, humanoid/robotics platforms
NOVT.key_suppliers: Specialty optics, magnets, semiconductor IC vendors, fabrication subcontractors
NOVT.robotnik_notes: Novanta's component portfolio (encoders, galvo scanners, lasers, servo drives) is heavily designed-in to medical-device and surgical-robot OEM platforms where regulatory revalidation creates multi-year switching cost, similar in spirit to the auto-MCU/ALGM logic. Competition from Coherent, IPG, Lumentum, MicroE and Renishaw exists at the component level, but design-win lifecycles are long and switching is qualification-intensive. Not a sole-source for any critical input, so MEDIUM rather than HIGH.

HSAI.bottleneck_description: Automotive ADAS lidar leader with ~33% overall, 43% long-range ADAS and 61% robotaxi share, but RoboSense, Huawei and Seyond contest the market and Chinese lidar supply is geopolitically gated for Western buyers.
HSAI.key_customers: Li Auto, Xiaomi, BYD, Geely, Chery, Zoox (Amazon), Aurora, WeRide, Pony, Apollo (Baidu), Didi
HSAI.key_suppliers: Sony/Sumitomo (lasers/photodetectors), Chinese optical component vendors, MEMS/SiPM suppliers
HSAI.robotnik_notes: Hesai is the world's #1 long-range ADAS and robotaxi lidar supplier (5 consecutive years), with 1.6M+ unit shipments and 4M-unit 2026 capacity plan, supplying Li Auto, Xiaomi, BYD, Zoox, Aurora, WeRide and Pony. However, RoboSense holds #1 passenger-car volume share, Huawei and Seyond are credible competitors, and customers routinely dual-source. Chinese-supplier dominance (95% of automotive lidar) creates geopolitical switching friction for Western customers (mirrors TSEM-type regional concentration logic). Not a structural monopoly so MEDIUM rather than HIGH.

JEN GR.bottleneck_description: Specialty optics, microoptics and beam-shaping subsystems co-designed with ASML for DUV/EUV lithography platforms, with a new ~EUR100M Dresden fab doubling micro-optics capacity.
JEN GR.key_customers: ASML, semiconductor inspection/metrology OEMs, defense/aerospace, automotive sensor/lidar customers
JEN GR.key_suppliers: Schott (optical glass), specialty coating chemistry vendors, precision mechanical subcontractors
JEN GR.robotnik_notes: Jenoptik supplies performance-critical, co-designed optical subsystems into ASML lithography and other semiconductor inspection/metrology platforms (DUV and EUV adjacent), and absorbed Berliner Glas optics from ASML in 2021. Qualification cycles for litho-grade optics are long (multi-year) and supplier base is limited, but Zeiss SMT remains the dominant projection-optics partner for ASML and other specialty-optics houses (Schott, Asphericon, Excelitas) exist. Real switching friction but not sole-source for EUV systems, so MEDIUM rather than HIGH.

OUST.bottleneck_description: Digital flash/spinning lidar for industrial, automotive and robotics, post Velodyne merger; ~$110-150M annualized revenue, sub-scale vs Chinese leaders Hesai and RoboSense.
OUST.key_customers: Warehouse automation, yard-logistics, smart city/infrastructure, select robotaxi pilots
OUST.key_suppliers: VCSEL/laser diode vendors, SPAD/sensor IC vendors, contract manufacturers
OUST.robotnik_notes: Post-Velodyne merger, Ouster competes in industrial, smart-infrastructure, automotive and robotics lidar against Hesai, RoboSense, Innoviz, Luminar, Aeva, Valeo and Continental. With Chinese suppliers holding ~95% of automotive lidar, Ouster's automotive position is marginal and its industrial/warehouse niche is contested. Q3 2025 revenue of $39.5M and improving gross margin (45%) signal product viability but no structural bottleneck. Conservative LOW; competitive market with realistic substitution.

2498 HK.bottleneck_description: World #1 passenger-car lidar by 2024 volume and growing robotics lidar leader (1,458% YoY Q1 2026 robotics growth) in a Chinese-dominated duopoly with Hesai.
2498 HK.key_customers: BYD, Geely, FAW, NIO, XPeng, Tier-1 robotics OEMs and humanoid integrators, 3,400+ robotics customers
2498 HK.key_suppliers: Lumentum/Sony laser components, optical assemblies, MEMS mirror vendors, Chinese photonic IC fabs
2498 HK.robotnik_notes: RoboSense is the #1 global passenger-car lidar by 2024 volume share and has rapidly expanded into robotics lidar (185,500 robotics units in Q1 2026, surpassing automotive). Combined with Hesai it forms an effective duopoly in Chinese-supplied automotive/robotics lidar, with 310+ automotive brand/Tier-1 design wins (BYD, Geely, FAW). Real but bounded switching friction — Hesai, Huawei and Seyond are credible alternatives; Western customers face geopolitical export constraints similar to TSEM. MEDIUM rather than HIGH given the duopoly structure and active competition.

6914 JP.bottleneck_description: Photoelectric, laser displacement and FA sensors plus security PIR sensors, competing with Keyence, Omron, SICK, Panasonic, Banner, Pepperl+Fuchs and Micro-Epsilon.
6914 JP.key_customers: Factory automation integrators, security/automatic door OEMs, electronics assembly customers in Japan/US/Europe/Asia
6914 JP.key_suppliers: Image sensor vendors, optical component suppliers, electronics CMs
6914 JP.robotnik_notes: Optex operates in highly fragmented industrial sensor categories (photoelectric, laser displacement, fiber, machine-vision lighting, security PIR) where the market leaders are Keyence, Omron, SICK and Panasonic; Optex is a mid-tier specialist with strong niches but no structural choke-point. Customers routinely qualify multiple vendors per sensor class with low switching friction. Aligns with the LOW frontier-stack baseline for peer-competitive industrial sensor incumbents.

BSL GR.bottleneck_description: World's largest unit-volume producer of digital industrial cameras (area-scan, line-scan, 3D, embedded vision), but heavily dependent on Sony CMOS sensors and competing with Teledyne, IDS, JAI, Allied Vision, Hikvision.
BSL GR.key_customers: Cognex (board-level), machine vision integrators, factory automation OEMs, life-science/medical imaging, retail/traffic
BSL GR.key_suppliers: Sony (Pregius/IMX CMOS image sensors), onsemi, FPGAs, optical lenses
BSL GR.robotnik_notes: Basler is the largest unit-volume maker of industrial machine-vision cameras in Europe, but the camera segment is highly contested by Teledyne DALSA, Sony, IDS, JAI, Allied Vision/FLIR, Hikvision/Hikrobot and Toshiba Teli. Basler is actually downstream of Sony's Pregius/IMX CMOS sensor monopoly-ish position; cameras are a mid-stack commodity-leaning subsystem with many substitution paths. No structural bottleneck — clear LOW.

098460 KS.bottleneck_description: Sole producer of 3D AOI inspection equipment with 52% global SPI share and 30% AOI share, 24,000+ installed base, dominant in 3D Moire SMT inspection.
098460 KS.key_customers: EMS providers (Foxconn, Jabil, Flex), automotive electronics, semiconductor advanced packaging customers, defense electronics
098460 KS.key_suppliers: CMOS image sensors, lasers, precision motion components, projection optics
098460 KS.robotnik_notes: Koh Young has held #1 global market share in 3D SPI (52%) and 3D AOI (30%) since 2006 and is described as the only producer of 3D AOI equipment using patented dual-projection Moire technology, with 24,000+ installed machines. Customers face real switching friction given installed-base inertia and 3D measurement workflow integration into SMT/advanced-packaging lines. However, 2D AOI and competing 3D systems from Test Research Inc (TRI), CyberOptics, Saki and Omron offer realistic substitution paths for many applications, so MEDIUM rather than HIGH. Aligns with MEDIUM anchor for structural duopoly/leader positions with viable but costly substitution.

6383 JP.bottleneck_description: Effective duopolist (with Murata Machinery) in semiconductor AMHS / overhead hoist transport (OHT) and FOUP-stocker systems inside 300mm/sub-3nm fabs, where vendor qualification and cleanroom integration create multi-year switching cost.
6383 JP.key_customers: TSMC, Samsung, Intel, Micron, SK hynix, flat-panel/OLED fabs (LG Display, Samsung Display), plus Amazon/airport/auto warehouse customers in non-cleanroom segments
6383 JP.key_suppliers: Motor and controls vendors (Fanuc, Yaskawa, Mitsubishi), bearings/precision mechanicals, cleanroom-grade enclosures, semiconductor controller chips
6383 JP.robotnik_notes: Daifuku is consistently cited alongside Murata Machinery as the global leader in semiconductor AMHS (OHT segment ~46% of AMHS spend), with SEMES/SFA only meaningful inside Korea. Fab AMHS is sticky: the rail network is embedded in the cleanroom and qualified to a tool layout, so swapping vendors mid-fab is impractical. However, Daifuku's intralogistics/auto/airport segments (~50%+ of revenue) face peer competition from Dematic/KION, Honeywell, SSI Schaefer and Murata, so the bottleneck only applies to roughly half the business. That mixed profile maps to the MEDIUM tier alongside AMAT/MU rather than the HIGH-tier sole-supplier anchors.

AUTO NO.bottleneck_description: Category-creator and leader in cube/grid ASRS with ~1,900 installations and a global integrator channel, but the same retrieval workload can be served by competing ASRS architectures (shuttles, mini-loads, robot AMR-to-rack) from many vendors.
AUTO NO.key_customers: Puma, Best Buy, Asda, Lidl, Gucci, H Mart, Siemens, plus white-label deployments through Dematic, Swisslog, Bastian, KNAPP and Element Logic
AUTO NO.key_suppliers: Aluminium grid extruders, lithium battery suppliers, wheel/motor vendors, IPC/PLC controllers, integrators provide site engineering
AUTO NO.robotnik_notes: AutoStore is the clear leader inside the narrow cube-storage sub-segment and the Ocado settlement gives both parties cross-licensed access to pre-2020 patents, so the legal moat has weakened. Outside the cube niche, customers can substitute Exotec Skypod, Geek+, Hai Robotics, AutoStore-style clones (Element Logic uses AutoStore but BMG and others build alternatives), shuttle ASRS from Dematic/SSI Schaefer/TGW, or traditional mini-loads — all competitive on $/throughput. The technology advantage is real but not a sole-source position. Aligns with the SYM LOW anchor (warehouse automation, contested).

KARN SW.bottleneck_description: One of the largest vertical lift module (VLM) / vertical carousel vendors with global reach via Kardex Remstar, competing with Modula, SSI Schaefer Logimat, Hänel and System Logistics in a product category with low switching cost.
KARN SW.key_customers: Manufacturing plants (Bosch, Siemens, automotive Tier-1s), MRO operations, healthcare distribution, e-commerce SKU pickers, Amazon US fulfillment (recently)
KARN SW.key_suppliers: Steel structures and tray suppliers, servo motors (Siemens, ABB), PLCs (Siemens, Rockwell), Mitsubishi/Fanuc controllers, lift hardware
KARN SW.robotnik_notes: VLMs are a discrete product class served by a roughly six-vendor field — Kardex Remstar, Modula, SSI Schaefer, Hänel, Ferretto, ICAM — with near-identical specs and pricing. Buyers cross-shop on price, service network and software integration; substitution is straightforward at the unit-purchase level. The recent AutoStore acquisition (Kardex bought Vertical Industries / Mlog and the AutoStore integrator footprint) expanded scope but not into a bottleneck position. Maps to LOW (peer-competitive intralogistics).

INRN SW.bottleneck_description: Global market leader in conveyor rollers and drum motors with a broad platform (>60,000 SKUs) sold to system integrators, but in a component category where Van der Graaf, Rulmeca, Damon, Titan and dozens of regional suppliers offer direct substitutes.
INRN SW.key_customers: Conveyor system integrators serving Amazon, DHL, FedEx, Coca-Cola, P&G, Walmart, airport baggage handlers, supermarket checkouts, mining/aggregates
INRN SW.key_suppliers: Steel tube mills, bearing manufacturers (SKF, NSK, Schaeffler), copper wire, electronic motor controllers, rubber/poly belt material
INRN SW.robotnik_notes: Conveyor rollers and drum motors are an established commodity-engineered category with multiple credible alternatives at every price point. Interroll's scale (~CHF 527M revenue, 36 subsidiaries) and platform breadth give it specification advantages with integrators, but switching to Van der Graaf, Rulmeca or regional alternatives is a parts-spec decision, not a multi-year qualification. Drum motor efficiency (~90%) is matched by peers. Maps to LOW (broad competitive component supply).

GMED.bottleneck_description: #2 spine surgical robotics platform (ExcelsiusGPS) in a clearly contested 4-5 player market against Medtronic Mazor, J&J VELYS, Stryker Mako Spine, and Zimmer Rosa Spine.
GMED.key_customers: Hospitals, ambulatory surgery centers (orthopedic surgery departments), spine surgeons
GMED.key_suppliers: Component suppliers for navigation cameras, robotic arms, contract manufacturers; pull-through with Globus implants/spinal hardware
GMED.robotnik_notes: Spine robotics is a peer-competitive oligopoly: Medtronic leads at ~22-24% share, Globus at ~16-18%, with J&J/Stryker/Zimmer all selling viable alternatives. While individual hospitals face real capital switching friction ($700K-$1.5M systems plus surgeon retraining), the market has 4-5 credible substitutes and no single platform is structurally indispensable. Globus's value comes from scale, IP, and integrated implant pull-through, not from being a sole-source bottleneck. Matches LOW calibration of peer-competitive system integrators (ABBN, 6954, ROK, SYM).

2252 HK.bottleneck_description: Chinese domestic challenger to Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci with its Toumai laparoscopic robot; only ~100 cumulative global orders as of late 2025 against a market overwhelmingly served by Intuitive.
2252 HK.key_customers: Chinese tertiary hospitals (primary), international hospitals adopting domestic-substitute robotic surgery, telesurgery pilot programs
2252 HK.key_suppliers: Domestic Chinese component manufacturers for robotic arms, optics, contract assembly
2252 HK.robotnik_notes: MedBot is structurally a challenger, not a bottleneck. The Chinese surgical robot market is dominated by Intuitive's da Vinci, with MicroPort, EdgeMed, KangDuo and other domestic players competing for the local-substitution opportunity. Toumai's NMPA approvals (urology 2022, expanded indications 2023, SP and tele-surgery 2025) make it a credible alternative within China, but the global laparoscopic robotic market has Intuitive as the dominant supplier with multiple emerging Chinese alternatives. Disruption of MedBot would have no meaningful downstream impact.

TECN SW.bottleneck_description: Lab automation/liquid handling vendor competing directly with Hamilton, Beckman Coulter, Thermo Fisher, Agilent, Eppendorf, and Revvity across the lab automation stack.
TECN SW.key_customers: Pharma R&D labs, clinical diagnostic labs, academic research institutions, CROs, biotech firms
TECN SW.key_suppliers: Component suppliers for motion control, optics, pipetting tips, contract manufacturers; OEM partners
TECN SW.robotnik_notes: Tecan is a strong #2/#3 in lab automation behind Thermo Fisher with Hamilton as its most direct liquid-handling competitor and several other large-cap players (Beckman/Danaher, Agilent, Eppendorf) selling overlapping platforms. While individual lab workflows have validated-method switching friction (assay re-qualification time), the market has multiple credible substitutes across modular liquid handlers, plate readers, and integration systems. No structural sole-sourcing dynamic; sits squarely with peer-competitive system integrators in the LOW calibration tier.

PRCT.bottleneck_description: AquaBeam/HYDROS Aquablation is the only robotic heat-free waterjet BPH therapy, but the broader BPH treatment market has many established alternatives (TURP, HoLEP, Rezum, UroLift, TULSA-PRO).
PRCT.key_customers: Hospitals, ambulatory surgery centers, urology practices treating BPH patients
PRCT.key_suppliers: Contract manufacturers for AquaBeam/HYDROS console and single-use disposable handpieces; imaging (ultrasound) component suppliers
PRCT.robotnik_notes: While PROCEPT is the sole vendor of its specific Aquablation modality, BPH is a treatment continuum with abundant clinical substitutes: Boston Scientific's Rezum (water vapor), Teleflex's UroLift (implants), HoLEP laser enucleation, traditional TURP, and Profound Medical's TULSA-PRO. From a supply-chain bottleneck perspective, displacement of PROCEPT would have no downstream supply-chain consequence — urologists would route patients to alternative therapies. The 'first/only' framing is therapeutic differentiation, not a structural bottleneck like ASML or 6920 JP. Therapy-area sole-source is not the same as supply-chain sole-source.

9660 HK.bottleneck_description: Leading Chinese ADAS SoC + software stack supplier with ~21% market share among Chinese OEMs and embedded Tier-1 design wins across BYD, Li Auto, SAIC, VW Carizon JV; switching cost rises with each model homologation.
9660 HK.key_customers: BYD, Li Auto, SAIC, GAC, Chery, Volkswagen Group (Carizon JV), Deepal, BAIC, Voyah, plus Tier-1s Bosch, Luxshare, Huaqin, TzTek
9660 HK.key_suppliers: TSMC (foundry for Journey SoCs), packaging/test partners, IP licensors (Arm, etc.)
9660 HK.robotnik_notes: Horizon is the largest domestic ADAS solutions provider in China and the dominant non-Tesla/non-Nvidia compute platform in the mid-tier (36% share at J5 level in 2024), with 290 model integrations across 27 OEMs and a $2.3B VW JV. However, it faces head-on competition from Nvidia DRIVE (Orin/Thor), Mobileye, Huawei MDC, Black Sesame and Tier-1 in-house chips, all of which are validated alternatives. The bottleneck position is structural in the Chinese localization wave (geopolitical preference, software-hardware integration, qualified design wins) but does not approach a sole-source or duopoly status. The auto-grade qualification cycle creates real switching friction once a model launches, consistent with the MEDIUM ALGM/ALGM-style anchor.

KDK.bottleneck_description: AI self-driving software stack (Kodiak Driver) for Class-8 trucks and military AGV applications; competitive autonomy-software market with multiple credible peers.
KDK.key_customers: Atlas Energy Solutions, U.S. Department of Defense, General Dynamics Land Systems (partnership), Verizon Business, freight shippers
KDK.key_suppliers: Nvidia (compute), Luminar/sensor vendors, OEM truck chassis providers, AWS/cloud compute
KDK.robotnik_notes: Kodiak operates in a multi-vendor autonomous-trucking market alongside Aurora (regarded as the leader), Plus (partnered with Traton/Navistar), Waabi, Gatik, and Embark legacy, plus OEM in-house programs. While Kodiak has differentiated wins (Atlas Energy customer-owned trucks, a ~$30M DoD contract, General Dynamics AGV collaboration, Verizon partnership), no single end-user is locked in and substitution paths exist. Its early defense-collaboration footprint and operational maturity are commercial strengths, not a bottleneck. The autonomy-software market is exactly the kind of contested frontier-stack baseline the framework labels LOW.

2431 HK.bottleneck_description: Mid-tier Chinese L2/L2+ ADAS domain-controller and DMS supplier; competitive design-win basis, partially backed by Horizon Robotics shareholding.
2431 HK.key_customers: Changan Automobile, multiple Chinese OEMs for L2/L2+ ADAS, Sterling Tools (India), export-model OEMs across EU/UK/Australia/SEA/Middle East/South America
2431 HK.key_suppliers: SoC suppliers (incl. Horizon Journey, NXP, Mobileye, TI), camera/sensor vendors, foundry partners via fabless chip suppliers
2431 HK.robotnik_notes: MiniEye is a credible but sub-scale Chinese ADAS supplier (Changan ADAS domain-controller win, Sterling Tools India partnership), competing directly with Horizon (which is now a strategic shareholder), Bosch, Huawei MDC, Black Sesame, Desay SV, ZF, Continental, and OEM in-house teams. Project-level switching cost exists but the broader market has many qualified suppliers, and MiniEye lacks unique IP or scale to be a sole-source bottleneck. The Horizon stake reinforces commercial linkage but does not change the structural position. Reflects a competitive mid-tier ADAS solutions market consistent with the LOW anchor for contested supplier categories.

RSW LN.bottleneck_description: World leader in machine-tool touch probes, CMM probes, optical/wireless transmission probes, and laser/encoder calibration; effective duopoly with Hexagon plus specialized peers (Heidenhain, Zeiss, Blum, Marposs).
RSW LN.key_customers: Boeing, Lockheed Martin (F-35), Ford, GM (EV battery), aerospace/auto Tier-1s, medical device manufacturers, semicap and machine-tool OEMs
RSW LN.key_suppliers: Optics/laser component suppliers, ASIC/electronics suppliers, precision-machining sub-suppliers, ruby/sapphire stylus material vendors
RSW LN.robotnik_notes: Renishaw is the industry standard for workpiece and tool probes on CNC machine tools, with deep CAM/CNC ecosystem integration (Boeing, Lockheed, Ford, GM, F-35) and a strong installed base in metrology. The probe/encoder market is moderately consolidated with Hexagon as the principal direct rival, plus Heidenhain (CNC-integrated probes), Zeiss (scanning/CMM), Blum-Novotest, and Marposs. Switching cost is meaningful (post-process inspection workflows, programming integration, brand reliability) but not prohibitive, and aerospace/auto buyers actively dual-source. The competitive structure (handful of qualified suppliers, real switching friction) is closest to the MEDIUM band rather than LOW or HIGH.

RPI LN.bottleneck_description: Low-cost single-board computer and RP2 microcontroller silicon for education, hobbyist, and OEM/IoT/industrial customers; structurally competitive SBC market.
RPI LN.key_customers: Educators, hobbyists, industrial-automation/IoT OEMs embedding Compute Module, home-automation/robotics integrators
RPI LN.key_suppliers: Sony (UK fab partnership for SBC assembly), Broadcom (SoCs for SBCs), TSMC (foundry for RP2 silicon), component distributors
RPI LN.robotnik_notes: Raspberry Pi has scale (>68M boards sold) and a strong software/community ecosystem advantage, but the SBC market includes Arduino, BeagleBone (incl. ruggedized BBBI), AAEON UP industrial boards, Orange Pi, Banana Pi, Rock Pi, and ARM/x86 industrial alternatives. Industrial OEMs increasingly favor rugged or x86 alternatives with longer lifecycle guarantees, and microcontroller competition (STM32, ESP32, NXP) is even more fragmented. No customer is locked in and substitution paths are abundant. Brand and ecosystem stickiness do not create a supply-chain bottleneck in the framework sense, so LOW is the calibrated rating.

AVAV.bottleneck_description: Dominant US-domestic supplier of Switchblade loitering munitions and tactical small UAS to US Army/DoD, with battle-tested program-of-record status that creates real qualification switching friction.
AVAV.key_customers: US Army, US Marine Corps, US Special Operations Command, Ukrainian Armed Forces (via FMS), allied NATO militaries
AVAV.key_suppliers: Various US-domestic electronics/composites suppliers; BlueHalo (post-acquisition) for space/cyber/directed energy; production capacity recently doubled to 2,000 units/month
AVAV.robotnik_notes: Switchblade has a real program-of-record moat in US loitering munitions (UVision and IAI exist but lack US production/DoD qualification at equivalent scale), and BlueHalo acquisition extends franchise into space/cyber/DE. However, the broader tactical UAS and loitering munition market is increasingly contested by Anduril, Shield AI, Kratos, Teal/Red Cat and low-cost FPV alternatives — the bottleneck is qualification and DoD relationship, not technological uniqueness. MEDIUM reflects real but contestable switching friction in a growing competitive field.

MBLY.bottleneck_description: Dominant ADAS vision SoC supplier with EyeQ family deployed in ~230M vehicles across ~1,200 vehicle models and >95% win rate at top OEM customers, creating multi-year automotive qualification switching cost.
MBLY.key_customers: VW Group, Stellantis, GM, Ford, BMW, Audi, Nissan, Honda, Hyundai, Geely and most other global OEMs ex-Tesla
MBLY.key_suppliers: STMicroelectronics (sole historical EyeQ SoC fabricator), TSMC (added for EyeQ6/imaging radar redundancy), Quanta Computer (ECU assembly)
MBLY.robotnik_notes: Mobileye is the closest analog to a structural ADAS oligopoly leader with auto-grade qualification creating prohibitive near-term switching cost (consistent with the ALGM/auto-MCU MEDIUM anchor). However, the broader ADAS-to-AD compute market is genuinely contested by Nvidia Drive (Mercedes, JLR, BYD wins), Qualcomm Snapdragon Ride (BMW, GM partial), Tesla in-house, Huawei MDC and Horizon Robotics in China — and Mobileye has been losing some China share.
