MEDIUM (not HIGH) reflects real switching cost on awarded programs but genuine multi-vendor competition for new design wins.

EXA FP.bottleneck_description: Top-tier global supplier of fiber-optic gyroscope inertial navigation systems, with vertically integrated FOG manufacturing and trusted-by-70-navies status creating multi-year qualification switching cost in maritime/defense INS.
EXA FP.key_customers: 70+ navies and armies globally including French Navy, Spanish Forces, US Navy (subsea), European tactical drone programs (Airbus), satellite primes (Astrix series for spacecraft attitude control)
EXA FP.key_suppliers: Vertically integrated; designs and manufactures FOG coils, accelerometers, electronics and algorithms in-house; minimal external dependency for core IP
EXA FP.robotnik_notes: Exail sits in a structural global top-3 FOG oligopoly with Honeywell and Safran (top 5 collectively ~70% of nav-grade revenue), and defense/space qualification creates prohibitive switching cost on awarded programs. However, this is a peer-competitive oligopoly — Honeywell, Safran, Northrop Grumman LITEF, and KVH all compete for new sockets, and ring-laser-gyro and MEMS IMU alternatives exist in lower-grade tiers. MEDIUM reflects real qualification moat consistent with structural-duopoly anchors but not a sole-source position.

EH.bottleneck_description: First and only eVTOL manufacturer worldwide to hold all four Chinese CAAC certificates (Type, Airworthiness, Production, Operational) for autonomous passenger air taxi, conferring a 12-24 month regulatory head-start in the China low-altitude economy market.
EH.key_customers: Guangzhou and Hefei municipal eVTOL operators (commercial ticketed flights at RMB299), Chinese tourism/sightseeing operators, future urban air mobility customers
EH.key_suppliers: Chinese domestic composites, battery cell, electric motor and avionics suppliers; specific component partners not publicly disclosed in detail
EH.robotnik_notes: EHang's quadruple CAAC certification (the first and currently only eVTOL company globally) creates a temporary structural bottleneck in Chinese passenger eVTOL operations. However, this is a regulatory-timing moat rather than a permanent supply-chain monopoly: AeroHT (XPeng), Autoflight, Volant Aerospace are in final certification stages, and the broader global eVTOL race includes Joby, Archer, Lilium and Vertical. Revenue base is still negligible and commercial scaling is unproven. MEDIUM (not HIGH) reflects a real but time-limited regulatory advantage in a market where viable peer-substitutes are 1-2 years away.

SERV.bottleneck_description: Largest US sidewalk delivery robot fleet (~2,000 units) with anchor Uber Eats partnership, operating in a contested last-mile autonomous delivery market with multiple peer alternatives.
SERV.key_customers: Uber Eats (anchor platform partner), DoorDash, Shake Shack, White Castle, regional restaurant brands across LA, Miami, Chicago, Dallas-Fort Worth, Atlanta
SERV.key_suppliers: Nvidia (compute), Magna International (manufacturing partner for Gen 3 robots), various sensor/lidar/camera suppliers (not single-sourced)
SERV.robotnik_notes: Sidewalk delivery is a competitive market with multiple credible operators (Starship Technologies with the largest global fleet, Coco Robotics, Kiwibot, Cartken/Mitsubishi, Avride/Yandex) and substitutes from drone delivery (Zipline, Wing) and human-courier gig platforms. Serve has scale-leader position in the US sidewalk niche but no proprietary bottleneck input, and the Uber Eats relationship is commercial rather than exclusive. LOW is consistent with the SYM warehouse-automation calibration anchor — contested operational-automation market with no structural choke-point.

9880 HK.bottleneck_description: One of several Chinese humanoid OEMs (Walker S series) competing with Unitree, Xpeng, Fourier, Agibot domestically and Tesla/Figure/Apptronik globally; no sole-source role in any downstream OEM supply chain.
9880 HK.key_customers: Dongfeng, BYD, Geely, Foxconn (humanoid pilots); Chinese education sector (Alpha/Cruzr); consumer Jimu kits
9880 HK.key_suppliers: Inovance Technology (servo motors), ZD Motor (joint modules), Green Harmonic / Leader Drive (harmonic reducers), domestic Chinese precision components
9880 HK.robotnik_notes: UBTECH is a humanoid system integrator that pilots Walker S units in Chinese auto plants (Dongfeng, BYD, Geely, Foxconn), but these are pilot deployments, not committed production-line dependencies. The company is a buyer of critical components (Inovance servos, ZD Motor joint modules, harmonic reducers) rather than a supplier of them, so any bottleneck rents accrue upstream. The humanoid OEM market is structurally crowded with multiple peers shipping at similar maturity. This places UBTECH below industrial-robot incumbents (Fanuc/ABB at LOW) on bottleneck dimensions because its end-customer commitments are still pre-commercial pilots.

688169 C1.bottleneck_description: Global #1 in robot vacuum unit share (~19-23%) but operating in a structurally contested consumer-appliance category with at least five well-funded peers; not a critical-input bottleneck for any downstream stack.
688169 C1.key_customers: Direct-to-consumer (Amazon, Tmall, JD.com, retail), Xiaomi (legacy OEM relationship)
688169 C1.key_suppliers: Chinese consumer-electronics supply chain (lidar modules, brushless motors, lithium cells, Qualcomm/MTK/Allwinner SoCs)
688169 C1.robotnik_notes: Roborock has won meaningful share gains against iRobot, but the robot vacuum market is fragmented with Ecovacs, Dreame, Xiaomi, Narwal, and Dyson all shipping competitive product with rapid SKU refresh cycles. The company is a branded consumer-goods finisher sourcing batteries, motors, lidar modules, and SoCs from commodity suppliers — none of its output is a sole-source input for another industry. Consumer end-markets see ~12 month design cycles and aggressive price competition, the antithesis of switching-cost moats. Clearly LOW.

6600 HK.bottleneck_description: Smart-home / consumer SwitchBot brand with a nascent humanoid (Onero H1) launched Q1 2026; competes with Roborock, Ecovacs, Dreame in consumer robotics — no critical-input role.
6600 HK.key_customers: Direct-to-consumer (Amazon, retail across 90+ countries); Apple/Google/Amazon smart-home ecosystem integrations
6600 HK.key_suppliers: Chinese consumer electronics supply chain (BLE/Wi-Fi SoCs, brushless motors, lithium cells, plastic injection)
6600 HK.robotnik_notes: Newly IPO'd (Dec 2025) consumer smart-home company best known for SwitchBot accessories, now extending into humanoid housekeepers. Operates in a hyper-competitive consumer electronics market with low switching costs and many peer brands. Despite 90-country distribution and 3.6M households served, products are discretionary consumer goods, not industrial inputs. Onero H1 is unproven at scale and ships into the same crowded humanoid consumer field. Clearly LOW.

RR.bottleneck_description: Small US service-robot integrator (ADAM coffee robot, Scorpion bartender, Titan delivery) with NVIDIA-based control stack; deployments are individually substitutable, no sole-source role.
RR.key_customers: Hospitality venues, ghost kitchens, healthcare facilities, retail spaces (US market)
RR.key_suppliers: NVIDIA (Jetson compute), US/Chinese component vendors, contract manufacturing for sub-assemblies
RR.robotnik_notes: Richtech sells service robots for hospitality (coffee, bartending, delivery) where customer commitments are individual contracts that can be terminated and replaced by alternatives (Bear Robotics, Pudu, Keenon, Savioke, or human staff). The Las Vegas 20K sqft expansion underscores that this is a niche scale operation, not a critical-stack supplier. Domestic assembly with NVIDIA Jetson-based controllers is a procurement choice, not a moat. Clearly LOW.

455900 KS.bottleneck_description: KAIST-spinout medical exoskeleton maker (WalkON Suit, Angel Suit, Angel Legs) targeting paraplegia rehab; competes with Ekso Bionics, ReWalk, Cyberdyne, Wandercraft, Suit-X.
455900 KS.key_customers: Korean rehab hospitals, mobility-impaired patients, defense/industrial wearable pilots
455900 KS.key_suppliers: Maxon/Faulhaber-class precision motors, harmonic reducers, IMU/load-cell vendors, Korean precision sub-suppliers
455900 KS.robotnik_notes: Angel Robotics is a niche rehabilitation exoskeleton vendor. Despite Cybathlon 2024 gold medal credentials, the medical exoskeleton market has multiple international competitors and the customer base (rehab clinics, individual patients) faces no switching cost beyond device-level qualification. The company is a downstream system integrator that buys actuators and sensors, with no upstream bottleneck role. Small-cap and pre-commercial scale further argues against any structural moat. LOW.

277810 KS.bottleneck_description: KAIST HUBO spinout, now 35%-owned by Samsung, with RB Series cobots and HUBO humanoid platform; competes with UR, Doosan, Techman, Fanuc CRX, ABB GoFa in cobots and with global humanoid pure-plays.
277810 KS.key_customers: Samsung Electronics (anchor), Korean industrial users, US distribution via Schaumburg, IL branch
277810 KS.key_suppliers: Vertical integration on actuators/encoders/controllers; harmonic reducer imports (Harmonic Drive Systems, Leader)
277810 KS.robotnik_notes: Samsung's largest-shareholder backing provides capital and a likely flagship customer, but this is a downstream relationship, not an upstream bottleneck. The cobot market is structurally contested (Universal Robots, Doosan, Techman, JAKA, Han's Robot) with sub-50% Rainbow share even in Korea. Vertical integration on actuators/encoders is a cost story, not a sole-source moat for downstream customers. HUBO humanoid line is a research platform, not committed production. Despite the Samsung halo, the structural position remains LOW alongside other peer-competitive robot OEMs (Fanuc, ABB at LOW per anchors).

108490 KS.bottleneck_description: Maker of Dynamixel all-in-one smart servo actuators widely used in research and education robots; competes with Maxon, Faulhaber, U2D2/Cubemars/Dephy in smart-servo categories.
108490 KS.key_customers: Academic and research robotics labs globally, ROS/OpenManipulator ecosystem, Korean delivery pilots
108490 KS.key_suppliers: Korean precision component supply chain (motors, encoders), in-house cycloidal Dynamixel Drive gearing
108490 KS.robotnik_notes: Dynamixel is well-known in the academic/educational robot ecosystem (TurtleBot, OpenManipulator), but smart servos are a contested category with multiple alternatives at varying price/performance points. Robotis is not a sole-source for any industrial humanoid OEM — production humanoids use proprietary actuators or harmonic-reducer + motor pairs from Harmonic Drive Systems, Nidec, or Chinese suppliers. The Dynamixel ecosystem stickiness in research labs is genuine but not a critical-stack bottleneck. Delivery robot business adds further contested SKUs. LOW.

6841 JP.bottleneck_description: Process automation, DCS, field instruments, and test/measurement equipment supplier competing in well-populated oligopolistic markets with multiple credible global alternatives.
6841 JP.key_customers: Hydrocarbon/chemical/oil & gas processors, power utilities, pharma manufacturers, semiconductor fabs (T&M), electronics manufacturers (power analyzers, oscilloscopes)
6841 JP.key_suppliers: Semiconductor component suppliers, silicon resonant sensor fabricators (internal), electronics ODM/EMS partners
6841 JP.robotnik_notes: Yokogawa is a top-tier global player but sits in structurally competitive markets across all of its segments. In DCS it is one of six major players (ABB, Emerson, Honeywell, Siemens, Schneider, Yokogawa) where the top five share ~60% of the market — competitive, not bottleneck. In oscilloscopes/T&M it ranks around #9 with low single-digit mindshare versus Keysight, Tektronix, R&S, Teledyne LeCroy. In field instruments (pressure transmitters, flow meters) it holds #2 share with Emerson, E+H, ABB, Siemens, Honeywell, Krohne all credible substitutes. Strong installed-base lock-in creates switching friction within process plants, but there is no segment where Yokogawa is a sole-source choke point — substitution is realistic at the next greenfield project. Lower bottleneck position than Advantest (6857 JP MEDIUM) which has tighter ATE duopoly dynamics.

454910 KS.bottleneck_description: Heavy-payload (20kg+) collaborative robot arms - a niche where Doosan leads but where Universal Robots (UR20), FANUC (CRX-25iA) and ABB now offer direct substitutes.
454910 KS.key_customers: Auto OEMs, palletizing/machine-tending end users, distributors in North America/Western Europe (~70% of revenue overseas); recent ONExia acquisition (Pennsylvania integrator, July 2025) expands U.S. channel
454910 KS.key_suppliers: Servo motors, harmonic reduction gears (Nabtesco/Harmonic Drive/Leaderdrive), encoders, controllers, MCUs - all multi-sourced commodities
454910 KS.robotnik_notes: Cobot market is structurally fragmented and competitive: Universal Robots (~15% share) leads, with Dobot, AUBO, JAKA, FANUC, ABB, KUKA, Yaskawa, Techman and Franka Emika all viable alternatives. Doosan is a relatively strong number 5 globally (~4-5% share) and a leader in the 20kg+ niche, but FANUC CRX-25iA and UR20 directly compete. This sits with the calibration anchors ABBN/6954 JP/6503 JP/ROK as a peer-competitive industrial automation vendor. The cobot arm itself is increasingly a commodity; durable advantage rests in software ecosystems and integrator networks, which UR's UR+ ecosystem currently leads.

2432 HK.bottleneck_description: General-purpose collaborative robots (3-20kg payload) and best-selling MG400 desktop robot - a contested space with multiple Chinese (AUBO, JAKA) and global (UR, FANUC, ABB) substitutes.
2432 HK.key_customers: Distributors and end users in 80+ countries; ~60% of revenue exported (unusually export-heavy for a Chinese cobot maker); education, light manufacturing, electronics assembly customers
2432 HK.key_suppliers: Largely vertically integrated - Dobot designs its own controllers, servo drives, and encoders; upstream rare-earth permanent magnets, harmonic reducers, MCUs and power electronics are multi-sourced
2432 HK.robotnik_notes: Despite Dobot's #2 global cobot share (~13%) behind Universal Robots, the cobot market is structurally fragmented. Three of the top four positions are Chinese (Dobot, AUBO, JAKA) with overlapping product lines, plus global incumbents (UR, FANUC, ABB, KUKA, Yaskawa, Techman, Doosan, Franka). Switching between cobot vendors is low-friction relative to industrial robots given simpler programming and shorter qualification cycles. Dobot's vertical integration of controllers/servos/encoders is a cost advantage, not a bottleneck for customers - substitutes are abundant. Maps directly to LOW calibration anchors (ABBN/6954 JP/SYM) as peer-competitive automation vendor.

GSAT.bottleneck_description: MSS L/S-band spectrum and Band 53/n53 licenses underpinning Apple's iPhone Emergency SOS service; substitute D2D paths exist but lock-in is multi-year.
GSAT.key_customers: Apple (anchor, ~85% capacity allocation), XCOM-Labs, Qualcomm, IoT and asset-tracking customers
GSAT.key_suppliers: MDA Space (next-gen satellites), Rocket Lab (satellite bus subcontractor to MDA), SpaceX (launch)
GSAT.robotnik_notes: Globalstar has allocated 85% of current and future network capacity to Apple's Emergency SOS, with Apple investing ~$1.1B plus taking a ~20% equity stake to fund the next-generation constellation. The MSS spectrum (including Band 53/n53) and ground infrastructure are unique to Globalstar and not readily replicable. However, Apple could theoretically migrate to AST SpaceMobile, Iridium, or Starlink Direct-to-Cell over a multi-year horizon, so this is a costly but not impossible switch. Conservative MEDIUM in line with AST SpaceMobile-style D2C moats one tier above peers but below true sole-source.

IRDM.bottleneck_description: Only truly global LEO L-band MSS constellation with cross-linked 66 satellites and globally allocated L-band spectrum at 1616-1626.5 MHz.
IRDM.key_customers: US Department of Defense (EMSS gateway), maritime/aviation operators, IoT integrators, Garmin (inReach)
IRDM.key_suppliers: Thales Alenia Space (NEXT satellites), SpaceX (launch), Qualcomm (NTN modems)
IRDM.robotnik_notes: Iridium operates the world's only truly global LEO mobile satellite voice/data network, with L-band spectrum that is less susceptible to weather/interference than Ku/Ka-band LEO competitors. Mission-critical maritime, aviation, defense, and IoT users rely on it for high-latitude and polar coverage that no terrestrial or single GEO operator can match. However, Starlink, Inmarsat, OneWeb and AST SpaceMobile compete in adjacent broadband and D2D, eroding pricing power on the higher-bandwidth side. Switching costs for embedded mission-critical users (DoD EMSS contract) are high but not prohibitive.

BKSY.bottleneck_description: High-revisit sub-meter optical earth-imaging constellation competing in a peer-competitive market with Planet, Maxar, Airbus, and emerging Asian operators.
BKSY.key_customers: National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), NGA, US DoD, international defense ministries, Palantir, Esri
BKSY.key_suppliers: LeoStella (satellite JV with Thales Alenia), SpaceX/Rocket Lab (launch), Sierra Space (sensors)
BKSY.robotnik_notes: BlackSky operates ~19 Gen-2 satellites with Gen-3 35cm-resolution birds deploying, serving mostly US/allied government customers (97% gov in FY24, 62% US). The competitive set is large and growing: Maxar (legacy hi-res leader), Planet Labs, Airbus Defence & Space, Capella (SAR), ICEYE (SAR), plus Asian entrants Axelspace and Hancom InSpace. Customers routinely multi-source imagery. This mirrors the PL calibration anchor (LOW for earth imaging).

VSAT.bottleneck_description: GEO Ka/L-band broadband (combined with Inmarsat) facing aggressive substitution from Starlink LEO and Eutelsat OneWeb across aviation, maritime, and government verticals.
VSAT.key_customers: Commercial aviation (Delta, JetBlue, United IFC), US DoD, maritime/government, Inmarsat enterprise base
VSAT.key_suppliers: Boeing (ViaSat-3 satellite bus), Airbus (older fleet), SpaceX/ULA (launch), ST Engineering iDirect (ground)
VSAT.robotnik_notes: Viasat's ViaSat-3 GEO satellites deliver >1 Tbps per bird, and the Inmarsat acquisition (May 2023) consolidated L-band MSS for safety services. However, Starlink's 7,000+ LEO satellites have rapidly captured maritime/aviation broadband share, and Eutelsat OneWeb competes in multi-orbit enterprise. IFC/IFE customers (JetBlue, Delta, etc.) are actively dual-sourcing. Safety-of-life GMDSS L-band on Inmarsat is more sticky but represents a small share of revenue. Overall structurally LOW given clear, deployed substitutes.

LUNR.bottleneck_description: Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) lander provider in a peer-competitive NASA program alongside Firefly, Astrobotic, Draper, and others.
LUNR.key_customers: NASA (CLPS, Near Space Network), US Space Force, US DoD, commercial payload customers
LUNR.key_suppliers: SpaceX (Falcon 9 launch), Northrop Grumman/Aerojet Rocketdyne (engines), Honeybee Robotics (drilling)
LUNR.robotnik_notes: Intuitive Machines has won five CLPS task orders and successfully landed two Nova-C missions, but the CLPS roster includes Firefly Aerospace (the only fully successful soft landing to date), Astrobotic, Draper, Masten, Lockheed Martin, and others. NASA explicitly multi-sources lunar landers to mitigate single-provider risk. While IM has a meaningful book of business including the Near Space Network contract, lunar payload delivery is a competitive market by design.

TSAT.bottleneck_description: Legacy GEO FSS operator pivoting to Lightspeed LEO constellation; capacity and customer set is substitutable with SES, Intelsat, Eutelsat OneWeb, and Starlink.
TSAT.key_customers: Bell Canada, Canadian government, US DoD (some), broadcasters, enterprise data customers
TSAT.key_suppliers: MDA Space (Lightspeed prime), SpaceX (launch), MELCO (older satellites)
TSAT.robotnik_notes: Telesat's existing GEO fleet competes directly with SES, Intelsat, Eutelsat, and ABS in fixed satellite services with no unique bottleneck position. The Lightspeed LEO constellation full-service date has slipped to end-Q1 2028 due to chip supply delays, and creditors are litigating over a September 2025 equity distribution to shield Lightspeed equity from $1.7B of debt maturing December 2026. Going-concern flag set: 2025 net loss of $530M, GEO revenue declining 25%+, refinancing or bankruptcy explicitly disclosed as a risk. Structural bottleneck rating remains LOW; financial distress flagged separately.

MNTS.bottleneck_description: Vigoride orbital transfer vehicle in a competitive in-space transportation market with D-Orbit, Launcher (Vast), Impulse Space, Exolaunch, and Spaceflight.
MNTS.key_customers: NASA (Juno RDRE payload), Spaceworks (COSMIC), commercial smallsat operators, hosted-payload defense customers
MNTS.key_suppliers: SpaceX (Transporter rideshare launch), water-plasma thruster vendors, off-the-shelf bus components
MNTS.robotnik_notes: Momentus operates Vigoride OTVs for last-mile orbital delivery, with $3.2M Q1 2026 revenue and a Vigoride 8 mission booked for early 2027. The company removed substantial-doubt going-concern language in Q1 2026 after a $25M PIPE and convertible debt cleanup, so I am NOT flagging going-concern despite historical distress. Structurally, in-space transportation is competitive with multiple commercial OTV providers and customers (NASA, ESA) actively multi-sourcing. Microcap scale ($50M mcap) and continuing operating losses keep this a fragile but not bottlenecked operator.

SPIR.bottleneck_description: 100+ satellite RO/AIS/RF data constellation competing with PlanetiQ, GeoOptics, Kleos, HawkEye 360, and Unseenlabs in weather and RF-geolocation data services.
SPIR.key_customers: NOAA, NASA, ESA, US Space Force, EUMETSAT, defense and intelligence agencies, Luxembourg Space Agency
SPIR.key_suppliers: Glasgow in-house satellite manufacturing, SpaceX/Rocket Lab (launch), commercial GNSS receivers
SPIR.robotnik_notes: Spire operates ~100 LEMUR cubesats providing GNSS radio-occultation weather data, AIS/ADS-B tracking, and RF intelligence. Competitors include PlanetiQ and GeoOptics (RO weather), HawkEye 360 and Unseenlabs (RF geolocation), Kleos Space (RF), and ORBCOMM (AIS). Government customers (NOAA, ESA, NASA, DoD) explicitly multi-source data buys to avoid single-vendor lock-in. RF geolocation and weather-data niches are competitive and growing, with no unique chokehold position. Microcap scale with persistent operating losses.

GILT.bottleneck_description: Tier-1 supplier of VSAT ground-segment platforms (SkyEdge IV/II-c) and electronically steered antennas for LEO/multi-orbit networks; Gogo exclusive ESA antenna provider for Galileo business aviation and a key OneWeb/Eutelsat LEO ground partner.
GILT.key_customers: Gogo (exclusive ESA antenna distribution for bizav/defense), Eutelsat OneWeb, US DoD (Satellite Transportable Terminals, CCT-series portable terminals via Gilat DataPath/Defense), satellite operators (Intelsat, SES, Telesat), telecom operators using VSAT backhaul.
GILT.key_suppliers: RF/MMIC component vendors, antenna phase-shifter ICs, contract manufacturers for hubs/modems, Israeli aerospace supply base.
GILT.robotnik_notes: Gilat occupies a defensible niche in ground-segment hubs, modems, and increasingly LEO-capable ESAs, where it competes with Hughes, Viasat, ST Engineering iDirect, and Comtech — a clear oligopoly, not a monopoly. The exclusive Gogo Galileo ESA arrangement and growing DoD portable-terminal business create switching friction (qualification, certifications), justifying MEDIUM rather than LOW. Not CRITICAL or HIGH because multiple credible substitutes exist for VSAT hubs and ESAs.

SPCE.bottleneck_description: Suborbital space-tourism operator (SpaceShipTwo / Delta-class), not a satellite communications provider; no supply-chain bottleneck role — service is a discretionary consumer experience with multiple emerging alternatives (Blue Origin New Shepard, future SpaceX/Polaris).
SPCE.key_customers: Private individuals (ticketed astronauts ~$450K/seat), research payload clients (NASA, universities) for microgravity experiments.
SPCE.key_suppliers: The Spaceship Company (in-house manufacturing arm), Aurora Flight Sciences/Bell Textron and Qarbon Aerospace for Delta-class production partners, hybrid rocket motor suppliers.
SPCE.robotnik_notes: SPCE is mis-cohorted as satellite communications — it operates a suborbital tourism vehicle with no satcom function. Bottleneck rating is LOW: no supply-chain criticality, tourism is fully substitutable by Blue Origin and other future entrants, and the company has disclosed substantial doubt about ability to continue as a going concern with commercial flights pushed to late 2026. Financial distress flagged separately; structural bottleneck position is weak regardless.

RDW.bottleneck_description: Sole supplier of Roll-Out Solar Array (ROSA/iROSA) deployable solar wings powering the ISS, Lunar Gateway PPE, and Axiom Station, with 300+ patents and 100% on-orbit success across 1,000+ missions.
RDW.key_customers: NASA, Axiom Space, Boeing, Maxar, Thales Alenia Space, US Space Force, ESA
RDW.key_suppliers: Solar cell vendors (Spectrolab, Azur Space), composite & substrate manufacturers, MOOG (collaborator on ELSA contract)
RDW.robotnik_notes: Redwire's ROSA/ELSA deployable solar arrays and in-space manufacturing IP (acquired via Deployable Space Systems) create real switching costs - qualification for crewed/long-duration platforms takes years and competitors Beyond Gravity and Airbus Defence & Space have different form factors. However, multiple deployable solar alternatives exist and RDW is one of several space-infrastructure component suppliers rather than a single chokepoint. MEDIUM reflects the qualification moat without overstating monopoly position.

VOYG.bottleneck_description: Defense and space-station component supplier (signals intelligence, GNC, life-support) leading Starlab commercial LEO station consortium - one of three competing NASA CLD bidders alongside Axiom and Orbital Reef.
VOYG.key_customers: NASA, US Air Force, Lockheed Martin, Palantir, Sierra Space, Northrop Grumman, intelligence community
VOYG.key_suppliers: Airbus, MDA Space, Mitsubishi (Starlab partners); diversified electronics and aerospace component vendors
VOYG.robotnik_notes: Voyager (NYSE-listed June 2025) is a diversified defense electronics and space-infrastructure integrator without a clearly dominant chokepoint product. Its Starlab project is in active competition with Axiom and the Blue Origin/Sierra Space-led Orbital Reef for NASA's Commercial LEO Destinations program - no exclusive franchise. Defense & National Security segment offers communications, GNC, and SIGINT modules where multiple primes compete. LOW reflects competitive landscape across both segments.

AVIO IM.bottleneck_description: Sole European prime for Vega-C small/medium launch and solid-rocket-motor propulsion (P120C boosters shared with Ariane 6), positioning Avio as the only ESA-funded sovereign small-launch and tactical solid-propellant capability in Europe.
AVIO IM.key_customers: European Space Agency, EU Commission (Galileo, Copernicus), Italian MoD, ArianeGroup (P120C boosters for Ariane 6), defense ministries (European + US tactical missile propulsion)
AVIO IM.key_suppliers: Europropulsion JV (with ArianeGroup) for solid motors, Italian/European aerospace supply chain, Snecma/Safran for upper-stage engines, Italian government-backed CDP financing
AVIO IM.robotnik_notes: Avio benefits from sovereign-launch policy: ESA has formally designated it as Vega launch service provider post-Arianespace split, and P120C solid boosters are dual-use for Ariane 6 and Vega-C, making it structurally embedded in European institutional access to space. It is also Europe's only tier-1 large solid-propellant prime, relevant for the K-defense-style European missile build-out. However, ESA's European Launcher Challenge (Isar Aerospace, RFA, Maiaspace, Orbex, PLD Space) is funded specifically to introduce competition, and SpaceX rideshare remains a commercial substitute for non-sovereign payloads. Regional monopoly with eroding moat = MEDIUM.

SATL.bottleneck_description: Sub-meter optical earth imaging where Satellogic competes directly against Maxar, Airbus, Planet, BlackSky and emerging sovereign constellations - no irreplaceable position.
SATL.key_customers: Strategic US defense/intelligence customer (undisclosed $30M AI contract), Government of Malaysia (via Uzma Berhad), Suhora (India distributor), Albania, various LATAM governments
SATL.key_suppliers: SpaceX (Transporter rideshare launches), in-house NewSat/NextGen satellite bus, in-house optics and AI payload
SATL.robotnik_notes: Satellogic targets sub-meter optical EO with a low-cost vertically-integrated bus and 'sovereign constellation' technology transfer model (Malaysia, Suhora/India deals). It is a price-competitive challenger, not a sole-source. Same competitive dynamics as PL but with weaker scale and a smaller fleet, so it inherits the LOW rating. Revenue base is small (~$10-30M deals) and customer concentration is high, but that is a financial/scale concern, not a structural bottleneck.

OVZON SS.bottleneck_description: Small Ku-band GEO SATCOM-as-a-service operator (one owned satellite Ovzon 3, plus leased Intelsat capacity) with proprietary mobile terminals serving defense/NATO customers in a crowded competitive field.
OVZON SS.key_customers: U.S. Department of Defense (historic anchor), Swedish FMV (1.04B SEK 2025 order), European NATO customer (240 MSEK Q4 2025), public-safety, NGO, and maritime.
OVZON SS.key_suppliers: Intelsat (leased transponder capacity), Maxar/SSL (Ovzon 3 satellite bus), launch providers (SpaceX launched Ovzon 3), terminal contract manufacturers.
OVZON SS.robotnik_notes: Ovzon competes head-on with Viasat-Inmarsat, SES, Iridium, and increasingly SpaceX/Starshield PLEO services in the DoD/NATO SATCOM-as-a-Service market — DoD's PLEO program alone expanded from $900M to $13B ceiling, signaling abundant alternatives. Their differentiation is the small high-throughput on-the-move terminal portfolio (T6/T7/P20/P30) which gives some product moat, but Ku-band GEO capacity is a commodity and customers have many viable substitutes. Not a structural choke-point; financial position has improved sharply in 2025 (revenue 735 MSEK, EBITDA +291 MSEK, 1B+ SEK backlog), so no going-concern flag warranted.

ENTG.bottleneck_description: Dominant supplier of high-purity contamination-control consumables (filters, FOUPs, liquid delivery, CMP slurries, advanced deposition materials) with single-sourced positions on multiple advanced-node process steps.
ENTG.key_customers: TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix, Micron, GlobalFoundries (all major foundries/IDMs)
ENTG.key_suppliers: Specialty resins, fluoropolymers, high-purity chemicals, internal fabrication; CMC Materials acquisition broadened internal sourcing
ENTG.robotnik_notes: Entegris holds 35-40% share in microcontamination control and is single-sourced on several advanced-node process consumables (fluoropolymer filters, FOUPs, certain CMP slurries). Content-per-wafer rises with node scaling, deepening lock-in. CHIPS Act funding ($75M memorandum) for Colorado Springs facility underlines US-strategic positioning. While competition exists from Pall, Merck KGaA, and CMC peers in some segments, qualification cycles and node-specific lock-ins justify HIGH.

WCH GR.bottleneck_description: One of two Western producers of semiconductor-grade hyperpure polysilicon (with Hemlock); supplies high-purity poly used at leading-edge logic and memory fabs.
WCH GR.key_customers: Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, GlobalWafers, Siltronic (wafer manufacturers); Intel, GlobalFoundries downstream
WCH GR.key_suppliers: Internal silicon metal sourcing, trichlorosilane production captive, energy (German power)
WCH GR.robotnik_notes: Wacker is the dominant Western supplier of electronic-grade polysilicon and together with Hemlock controls roughly three-quarters of the semiconductor-grade poly market. With Chinese poly (GCL, Tongwei) primarily solar-grade and the US Section 232 investigation reinforcing Western sourcing preference, Wacker is structurally embedded in the semiconductor wafer supply chain. Capacity expansion plus shift away from solar-grade reinforces semi-criticality. HIGH rather than CRITICAL because Hemlock provides genuine alternative.

4043 JP.bottleneck_description: Top global producer of high-purity TMAH photoresist developer for EUV/advanced-node lithography plus semiconductor-grade polysilicon (~12,500 MT capacity, 7nm-and-below grade).
4043 JP.key_customers: TSMC, Samsung, leading-edge foundries via wafer/resist channels; Japanese and Korean fabs primarily
4043 JP.key_suppliers: Trichlorosilane/silicon metal captive production, specialty chemicals
4043 JP.robotnik_notes: Tokuyama is a major TMAH developer supplier (top-5 controls ~56% share) and a credible semiconductor-grade polysilicon producer alongside Wacker and Hemlock. Asia-Pacific dependence on Tokuyama for TMAH at advanced nodes is real. However, alternatives exist (Greenda, Hantok, Tama, SACHEM in TMAH; Wacker, Hemlock in poly), making MEDIUM the disciplined call. Switching is multi-quarter qualification but feasible.

SOI FP.bottleneck_description: Sole-source supplier of RF-SOI wafers for 5G smartphone front-ends and the only volume-qualified supplier of photonics-grade SOI wafers used in AI photonics chips, protected by ~4,300 Smart Cut patents.
SOI FP.key_customers: Qualcomm, Skyworks, Qorvo, Broadcom (RF-SOI); STMicroelectronics, GlobalFoundries (FD-SOI); TSMC, Intel, Tower (photonics-SOI for AI optical transceivers)
SOI FP.key_suppliers: Shin-Etsu/SUMCO (bulk silicon wafers as substrate), captive Smart Cut process
SOI FP.robotnik_notes: Soitec holds ~80% of total SOI wafers and BofA estimates >95% in photonics-grade SOI; >70% RF-SOI share for 5G smartphones. Smart Cut process is patent-protected (4,300 patents) with no equivalent process at volume. Photonics-SOI for AI optical transceivers is a sole-source dependency for the AI scale-up roadmap with no qualified second source today. RF-SOI and photonics-SOI together meet the calibration bar for CRITICAL (sole-source, no viable substitute today).

MP.bottleneck_description: Only scaled US mine-to-magnet NdPr producer; sole operator of Mountain Pass (the only US rare earth mine) with DoD-backed integrated separation and Fort Worth/Independence magnet build-out.
MP.key_customers: US DoD (price-floor offtake), GM, Independence magnet customers; Chinese sales (Shenghe) ceased July 2025
MP.key_suppliers: Internal Mountain Pass concentrate; reagents from US chemical suppliers
MP.robotnik_notes: MP operates the only commercially producing US rare earth mine and is the West's only vertically integrated mine-to-magnet NdPr entity outside China. The July 2025 DoD partnership (10-year $110/kg NdPr floor, $400M preferred equity, $150M heavy rare earth separation loan, 10X magnet facility commissioning 2028) cements its strategic-bottleneck status for US defense and EV magnet sovereignty. Lynas is the only credible substitute outside China; otherwise the West has no scaled alternative, hence HIGH rather than CRITICAL (a viable alternative exists in Lynas).

LYC AU.bottleneck_description: Only scaled rare-earth separator outside China and the first commercial producer of separated heavy rare earths (dysprosium, terbium) ex-China.
LYC AU.key_customers: JARE (JOGMEC/Sojitz), Japanese magnet makers, US DoD-funded Texas separation, European auto/wind OEMs
LYC AU.key_suppliers: Internal Mt Weld ore; reagents, fuel, regional power
LYC AU.robotnik_notes: Lynas operates the only fully integrated mine-to-separated-oxide rare earth supply chain outside China (Mt Weld mine, Kalgoorlie cracking-and-leaching, Malaysia separation, Kalgoorlie heavy REE expansion). First Dy shipments achieved 1H FY26, Tb following, with the JARE/Japan offtake extended to 2038 at a $110/kg NdPr floor. With China dominating ~90% of separation and Beijing imposing heavy-REE export controls, Western OEMs (Japan, US DoD, EU) have effectively no other near-term option — multi-year qualification and capital-intensity make substitution prohibitive. HIGH is appropriate (CRITICAL reserved for sole-source feedstock like 600111 C1).

ARU AU.bottleneck_description: Future NdPr producer at Nolans (NT) with multi-sovereign ECA financing and binding offtakes to Hyundai/Kia/Siemens Gamesa/Traxys; first production mid-2029.
ARU AU.key_customers: Hyundai, Kia, Siemens Gamesa, Traxys (500tpa NdPr + 7.5tpa DyTb)
ARU AU.key_suppliers: Internal Nolans deposit (pre-production); Australian engineering contractors
ARU AU.robotnik_notes: Nolans achieved FID with A$1.6B fully funded (Hancock at 17.5%, multi-sovereign ECA syndicate, NAIF, Strategic Reserve eligibility) and ~93% offtake target contracted. Strategically important as one of very few Western NdPr projects, but it is pre-production until 2029, so it does not yet exert a bottleneck. MEDIUM reflects the strategic position once online combined with execution and dilution risk. Not flagging going-concern: capital is now in place per recent A$350M placement and Hancock underwrite, though equity holders face material dilution.

ILU AU.bottleneck_description: World's largest zircon producer (~20% global share) and developer of Australia's first integrated rare earths refinery at Eneabba (2027 start) under a A$1.65B Australian Government Critical Minerals Facility loan.
ILU AU.key_customers: Pigment producers (Chemours, Kronos, Tronox), ceramic tile makers, foundry; future REE customers TBD
ILU AU.key_suppliers: Internal mineral sands stockpiles; Northern Minerals third-party REE feed; Fluor EPCM
ILU AU.robotnik_notes: Iluka has dual bottleneck dimensions: zircon/mineral sands (Jacinth-Ambrosia, Balranald) where it is the largest single producer but with global substitutes (Rio/Tronox/Kenmare/Base Resources); plus a near-term, government-funded integrated REE refinery at Eneabba that will be one of the few non-Chinese light+heavy REE separation facilities. Today, neither line individually qualifies as HIGH (zircon is competitive; REE refinery is pre-commissioning, slipped to 2027 with capex now A$1.7-1.8B). MEDIUM is appropriate — strategic Western critical-minerals infrastructure but with viable substitution and execution risk.

5706 JP.bottleneck_description: ~95%+ global share of MicroThin ultra-thin copper foil with carrier — the enabling input for HDI substrates, ABF/IC substrates, and advanced packaging (CoWoS/SLP/MSAP) used in AI accelerators.
5706 JP.key_customers: Substrate makers (Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB, AT&S), HDI PCB makers, automotive electronics, EV battery materials customers, exhaust catalyst auto OEMs
5706 JP.key_suppliers: Copper cathode feedstock, zinc/lead concentrate from Mitsui group mines, indium/tantalum/tin for functional materials
5706 JP.robotnik_notes: Mitsui Kinzoku is effectively a near-monopoly supplier of carrier-attached ultra-thin copper foil (<=5um) used in the highest-density semiconductor packaging substrates and HDI smartphone boards — the very materials that gate CoWoS, FC-BGA, and advanced AI-server substrates. Lower-tier peelable copper foil has alternatives at JX Nippon Mining & Furukawa, but Mitsui dominates the leading-edge MicroThin tier the AI substrate roadmap depends on. Not rated CRITICAL because substitutes exist at lower-tier nodes and Mitsui has been adding capacity, but the AI-packaging dependency is real and switching cost (re-qualification at substrate makers Ibiden/Unimicron/Shinko) is multi-year.

AMG NA.bottleneck_description: Largest US ferrovanadium producer + global #1 spent-catalyst recycler (V-CYCLE) + titanium aluminide / aluminum master alloys to aerospace engines + AMG Technologies vacuum furnace equipment to engine forgers.
AMG NA.key_customers: Aerospace engine OEMs and forgers (via AMG Technologies furnaces and TAC master alloys), oil refiners (catalyst recycling feedstock), steel mills (ferrovanadium), tier-1 battery makers (lithium concentrate)
AMG NA.key_suppliers: Oil-refinery spent catalyst (long-term recycling contracts), Brazilian tantalum ore (AMG Brasil), Brazil lithium spodumene (Mibra mine), chrome ore
AMG NA.robotnik_notes: AMG owns multiple niche-leadership positions: world's largest spent-catalyst vanadium recycler, largest US ferrovanadium producer (60kt/yr in Zanesville, OH), and a meaningful share of qualified titanium master alloys (AMG TAC Nuremberg) and chrome metal for nickel superalloys serving aero engine programs. Switching costs are real in aero-qualified master alloys and chrome metal for Ni-superalloys, but global ferrovanadium has Chinese and South African competitors and lithium/tantalum segments are not market-leading. Not HIGH because the portfolio is genuinely competitive at the alloy commodity level; not LOW because the spent-catalyst recycling and US ferrovanadium positions plus aero master alloy qualification provide real choke-point bite.
AMG NA.parent_basis_note: Dutch-domiciled parent (AMG Critical Materials N.V.) listed on Euronext Amsterdam (AMG NA); rating reflects parent consolidated position.

WAF GR.bottleneck_description: #4 global 300mm silicon wafer supplier (~12% revenue share) inside a 5-player oligopoly (Shin-Etsu/SUMCO/GlobalWafers/Siltronic/SK Siltron) controlling ~85% of 300mm capacity.
WAF GR.key_customers: TSMC, Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron, Intel, Infineon, STMicro (memory + logic + power)
WAF GR.key_suppliers: Polysilicon producers (Wacker, OCI, GCL), quartz crucibles, slurry/CMP consumables, specialty gases
WAF GR.robotnik_notes: Siltronic sits in the same consolidated wafer oligopoly anchored at MEDIUM for Shin-Etsu — qualification cycles for prime 300mm wafers run multi-year and capital intensity is severe, but customers can dual-source across Shin-Etsu/SUMCO/GlobalWafers/SK Siltron. 2026 guidance flagged mid-single-digit revenue decline and net debt rose to EUR 837M on heavy capex; management noted peers being 'extremely vocal' about 200mm headwinds. Not a sole-source choke; calibration vs the Shin-Etsu MEDIUM anchor implies a smaller-share oligopoly participant should also rate MEDIUM rather than higher.

OLED.bottleneck_description: Near-monopoly licensor and supplier of phosphorescent red/green OLED emitter materials and IP, with a patent estate of 7,000+ issued/pending worldwide that gates panel-maker bills of materials.
OLED.key_customers: Samsung Display, LG Display, BOE Technology, CSOT, Visionox, Tianma, JOLED legacy IP licensees
OLED.key_suppliers: PPG Industries (exclusive emitter material manufacturing partner), specialty organic-chemistry CDMOs
OLED.robotnik_notes: UDC is the de facto sole commercial supplier of phosphorescent (PHOLED) red and green emitters used across virtually all modern AMOLED displays for smartphones, TVs, and IT panels; competing emitters from Japan/Korea remain hemmed in by cross-licensing. Long-term supply/license agreements with LG Display (extended through 2030), Samsung Display, BOE, and CSOT cement the position, supporting ~42% operating margins. The reason this sits at HIGH (not CRITICAL) is that core patents begin to sunset late-decade and blue PHOLED commercialization is still in qualification — but through the 2026 horizon the chokepoint is real and structural.

6488 TT.bottleneck_description: #3 global 300mm silicon wafer supplier (~17% revenue share) inside the 5-player Shin-Etsu/SUMCO/GlobalWafers/Siltronic/SK Siltron oligopoly that controls ~85% of capacity.
6488 TT.key_customers: TSMC, Samsung, Intel, Micron, SK Hynix, Texas Instruments, GlobalFoundries, Infineon, onsemi
6488 TT.key_suppliers: Polysilicon (Wacker, OCI, Hemlock, Tokuyama), quartz crucibles, CMP slurry, specialty gases
6488 TT.robotnik_notes: GlobalWafers is a meaningful member of the consolidated silicon-wafer oligopoly anchored at MEDIUM (Shin-Etsu). Multi-year qualification cycles, severe capital intensity (its Sherman, TX phase-2 expansion is part of a $7.5B program), and tight 300mm capacity create real switching frictions, but customers can dual-source across at least four other prime wafer suppliers. The Sherman fab and the US CHIPS Act anchoring give it slight strategic premium as the leading non-Japanese/non-Korean US-domiciled 300mm supplier, but not enough to lift above MEDIUM under the conservative framework.

6723.bottleneck_description: Japanese auto + industrial MCU supplier — part of the auto-MCU oligopoly with multi-year qualification cycles and tight Tier-1 relationships.
6723.key_customers: Toyota, global Tier-1 auto suppliers, industrial OEMs
6723.robotnik_notes: Auto MCU is structurally a 4-player oligopoly (Renesas, NXP, Infineon, ST). Mid-platform switching is multi-year due to functional-safety qualification (ISO 26262) and software-stack porting. Revised from LOW given the auto-qualification switching cost dynamic that LOW under-weighted.

189300 KS.key_customers: Maritime fleets, defense/government, enterprise VSAT, LEO ground terminals (OneWeb/multi-orbit)
189300 KS.key_suppliers: RF/microwave components, phased-array & antenna materials, BUC/LNB modules
189300 KS.robotnik_notes: Leading maritime & enterprise satcom terminal maker (VSAT, flat-panel/phased-array antennas). Positioned in the LEO ground-segment buildout; terminal supply is a quiet enabler of the satellite-connectivity layer.

CBRS.key_customers: Sovereign-AI & hyperscale (G42/Gulf), national labs, pharma/genomics, LLM developers
CBRS.key_suppliers: TSMC (wafer fab), advanced packaging/substrate, HBM/SRAM, power & cooling
CBRS.robotnik_notes: Differentiated wafer-scale AI compute (WSE-3/CS-3); frontier-relevant but substitutable (NVIDIA-dominant + AMD/TPU/Groq) and downstream of TSMC/CoWoS/HBM. MEDIUM re-validated at IPO.

186A JP.bottleneck_description: On-orbit servicing and active debris-removal operator (ADRAS-J, ELSA, life extension); holds flown rendezvous-and-proximity-operations heritage but no concentrated supply-chain position.
186A JP.key_customers: JAXA, US Space Force, ESA / UK Space Agency, Eutelsat (life extension)
186A JP.robotnik_notes: Astroscale has genuine first-mover flight heritage: ADRAS-J is the first spacecraft to safely approach and characterise a large piece of orbital debris. That is a capability lead, not a control point. On-orbit servicing is an emerging, contestable service and the anchor customers deliberately multi-source it; the US Space Force ran its Tetra refuelling demonstrations across Astroscale, Northrop Grumman and Orbit Fab, and Northrop's life-extension vehicle is already operational. It fails the concentration and in-volume-dependence tests, so it rates LOW, the strongest of a weak-choke set. Revenue is demonstration and government-anchored rather than recurring.

290A JP.bottleneck_description: SAR (synthetic-aperture radar) smallsat Earth-observation constellation (StriX) and analytics; a differentiated modality but fungible among SAR peers.
290A JP.key_customers: Japan Ministry of Defense, Japan Air Self-Defense Force
290A JP.robotnik_notes: SAR imagery is all-weather and works day or night, but among SAR providers the data is largely interchangeable on resolution and revisit. The decisive fact against a choke-point reading is that Japan's Ministry of Defense deliberately multi-sourced its constellation programme across several firms, buying the same capability from Synspective and its direct competitor iQPS at once. Competitors ICEYE, Capella and Umbra supply the same modality. The sovereign-defence backlog is real franchise strength, not a control point, so LOW.

464A JP.bottleneck_description: SAR smallsat Earth-observation constellation (QPS-SAR); the same all-weather modality as Synspective, at an earlier build stage.
464A JP.key_customers: Japan Ministry of Defense (satellite-constellation programme, joint award)
464A JP.robotnik_notes: iQPS is one of several qualified SAR providers and is treated as interchangeable by its anchor customer: it was a co-awardee alongside Synspective and others in Japan's Ministry of Defense constellation tender. The same substitutes apply (ICEYE, Capella, Umbra, Synspective), and the business is a capital-intensive constellation build ahead of revenue. No concentrated, hard-to-route-around input, so LOW.

9348 JP.bottleneck_description: Commercial lunar landing and cislunar transport (HAKUTO-R); pre-revenue, with no successful landing to date and a contested, multi-sourced customer base.
9348 JP.robotnik_notes: Lunar delivery is a race among several providers, not a choke point, and NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme spreads awards across the field. ispace has attempted two landings and lost both, the June 2025 Resilience mission failing on descent, while competitors Firefly and Intuitive Machines have landed, and the June 2026 CLPS award went to Astrobotic, Firefly and Intuitive Machines with ispace absent. It holds no scarce input the stack depends on, so LOW with high confidence. Repeated capital raises fund the next attempts against a twice-failed core capability; key suppliers are not disclosed at a sourceable level and are left unstated rather than inferred.

ETL FP.bottleneck_description: European satellite operator running a GEO fleet plus the Eutelsat OneWeb LEO constellation; the only at-scale allied non-Starlink low-earth-orbit broadband network in service today.
ETL FP.key_suppliers: Airbus OneWeb Satellites (satellite manufacture), Arianespace and SpaceX (launch)
ETL FP.robotnik_notes: Outside China, Eutelsat OneWeb is the only fully deployed non-Starlink global LEO network, which gives it a genuine sovereignty position: a European government or institution that requires an allied, non-US LEO network today has few alternatives before Amazon Kuiper and the EU IRIS2 constellation mature later this decade. That is what lifts it above the LOW band of substitutable operators. It is capped at MEDIUM because commercial capacity is fungible, Starlink is a far larger competitor, and the sovereignty premium is strategic rather than a sole-source input. The balance sheet is heavily leveraged and has required state-backed recapitalisation, which reinforces the sovereign role while signalling financial strain.

FLY.bottleneck_description: US launch and space-services company (Alpha small-lift, Blue Ghost lunar lander, Elytra orbital transfer, Eclipse medium-lift with Northrop Grumman); the first commercial operator to complete a fully successful lunar soft landing.
FLY.key_customers: NASA (CLPS), US Space Force, US Department of Defense / DIU, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman
FLY.robotnik_notes: Firefly's one distinctive asset is being the only commercial entity with a proven, fully successful lunar landing (Blue Ghost, March 2025), and it is the sole-source domestic first-stage supplier for Northrop Grumman's Antares 330 and Eclipse. Both are real, but neither is route-around-proof: NASA deliberately multi-sources lunar delivery through CLPS, and the Alpha launch business is openly contested by Rocket Lab and SpaceX rideshare with a mixed reliability record. The deepest dependency actually runs the wrong way, with a heavily concentrated US-government customer base. Niche leadership with real switching costs rather than a choke point, so MEDIUM, on the Rocket Lab calibration. Engines and stages are built in-house; no external supplier is disclosed at a sourceable level.

KTOS.bottleneck_description: US defence-technology firm spanning aerial target drones, tactical jet drones, solid rocket motors and hypersonics, C5ISR and satellite ground systems; near-sole supplier of high-performance aerial targets to the US Air Force.
KTOS.key_customers: US Air Force, US Navy, US Department of Defense (MACH-TB hypersonic test bed)
KTOS.robotnik_notes: Kratos holds one genuine choke-point pocket: it is the dominant, effectively single-source supplier of US Air Force aerial target drones (BQM-167), where qualifying an alternative line would take years. That pocket alone would read HIGH. Against it, the rest of a diversified portfolio is contested; in solid rocket motors Kratos is the challenger trying to break the incumbent duopoly rather than the incumbent, and its Valkyrie tactical drone and ground-systems lines face active competition. Rated on the blended position the company lands MEDIUM, the treatment applied to other diversified niche-leaders, with the target-drone franchise noted as the sharp pocket. Heavy ITAR exposure runs across targets, hypersonics and motors.

MDA CN.bottleneck_description: Canadian space-systems prime across space robotics (Canadarm heritage), SAR Earth observation (RADARSAT) and satellite systems (Aurora bus, phased-array antennas); sole-source builder of Canada's flagship robotics.
MDA CN.key_customers: Canadian Space Agency (Canadarm3), NASA (Canadarm2 / Gateway via CSA), Telesat (Lightspeed), Globalstar
MDA CN.robotnik_notes: MDA's robotics line is a sovereign-locked choke point: Canadarm3 is Canada's designated national contribution to the Lunar Gateway, contracted sole-source and effectively impossible to re-source to a non-Canadian firm without unwinding an international agreement. That pocket reads HIGH, arguably higher within the Canada and Gateway lane. The bulk of MDA's growth, however, sits in competitive markets, satellite buses and antennas for Telesat Lightspeed and Globalstar, where customers have alternatives such as Airbus and Thales Alenia Space. Blended, the company rates MEDIUM, with the sovereign robotics franchise as the sharp pocket. Programme-concentration risk attaches to the repeatedly re-scoped Lightspeed constellation.

SESG FP.bottleneck_description: Luxembourg-based global satellite operator (GEO fleet plus O3b mPOWER MEO constellation), enlarged by the 2025 Intelsat acquisition; a scaled operator in a substitutable market.
SESG FP.key_customers: US Government / US Department of Defense (SES Space & Defense)
SESG FP.key_suppliers: Boeing (O3b mPOWER satellites), Thales Alenia Space (GEO satellites)
SESG FP.robotnik_notes: SES operates the one commercial medium-earth-orbit broadband constellation (O3b mPOWER), a genuinely distinct architecture, and its defence arm carries US-government accreditation that raises the barrier to entry. Neither makes it a control point: connectivity capacity is broadly fungible across Eutelsat OneWeb, Viasat, Starlink and Telesat, and the low-latency case that MEO was built to own is increasingly captured by LEO. Consistent with how other scaled operators are treated, it rates LOW. The mPOWER fleet has suffered power-system anomalies and the Intelsat integration adds debt and execution risk.

SIDU.bottleneck_description: US micro-cap smallsat manufacturer and space-data services company (3D-printed structures, LizzieSat); no sourced concentration position, rated conservatively on thin evidence.
SIDU.robotnik_notes: Sidus is a small, vertically integrated smallsat builder and aspiring data provider competing against many smallsat manufacturers and a crowded Earth-observation field; nothing about it is hard to route around. No market-share or sole-source position could be sourced, and named customer contracts could not be confirmed to a sourceable standard, so both the customer and supplier lists are left unstated rather than populated by inference. Micro-cap space companies of this profile commonly carry dilution and going-concern pressure, but those specifics could not be verified here and are therefore not asserted. Rated LOW with low confidence, reflecting the structural absence of any choke role together with the thin evidentiary base.

010060 KS.bottleneck_description: Korean chemicals group; via OCI Company Ltd it makes solar- and semiconductor-grade polysilicon plus phosphoric acid and specialty gases. Non-China supply optionality but no concentrated, hard-to-substitute position.
010060 KS.key_customers: SK Hynix (semiconductor-grade phosphoric acid), CubicPV (polysilicon offtake), Nexeon (monosilane)
010060 KS.robotnik_notes: Solar polysilicon is commoditised and roughly nine-tenths China-controlled, and OCI fell out of the global top ten producers in 2023; in semiconductor-grade polysilicon the leaders are Wacker, Hemlock and Tokuyama, with OCI a secondary source. Its one genuine lift is scarce non-China, forced-labour-clean supply plus qualified niches such as semiconductor-grade phosphoric acid to Korean memory makers, but that value is policy-contingent (US import and Section 232 measures) rather than a structural choke. Rated LOW: no concentrated position others cannot route around. It would rise to MEDIUM only if the non-China scarcity premium is weighted heavily.
010060 KS.parent_basis_note: 010060 KS is OCI Holdings, a holding company; the polysilicon and chemicals operations sit in OCI Company Ltd. Rated on the consolidated operating basis, with the choke-point logic attaching one level down.

3436 JP.bottleneck_description: World's second-largest silicon-wafer maker (300mm prime and epitaxial wafers), the substrate under essentially all leading-edge logic and memory.
3436 JP.key_customers: NXP, Infineon, SK Hynix, major Taiwanese foundries
3436 JP.robotnik_notes: Prime 300mm wafers are made at scale by only about five firms, and Shin-Etsu with SUMCO account for roughly half the market, so the concentration is a tight oligopoly rather than a monopoly. Every advanced logic, AI and HBM device starts on one of these wafers, making the volume dependence total, but customers deliberately multi-source and a credible named second source, Shin-Etsu, is qualified at every fab, even though switching carries multi-quarter to multi-year qualification. This is the same structure as Shin-Etsu, which is already rated MEDIUM, so SUMCO rates MEDIUM for parity. Clean operating entity with no export-control choke-point role.

4062 JP.bottleneck_description: Leading maker of the highest-complexity FC-BGA / ABF IC package substrates that carry the largest AI accelerators and data-centre CPUs; ABF substrate is a named frontier choke-point.
4062 JP.robotnik_notes: Ibiden holds the majority of the top tier of organic package substrates, the very high-layer-count, large-body parts the biggest AI GPU packages require, a segment that is sold out. Competitors exist (Shinko, Unimicron, AT&S, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Nan Ya) but are described as roughly a generation behind at that leading edge, and Ibiden secures close to all orders for the high-end generative-AI server substrates against demand-constrained supply, so customers cannot route around it there. It rates HIGH, short of CRITICAL only because alternatives are being qualified. The substrate is built on Ajinomoto build-up film upstream, itself an even tighter choke-point with Ajinomoto supplying the large majority of that film; the automotive-ceramics segment does not dilute the rating, which attaches to the substrate business that provides the majority of both sales and profit.

4186 JP.bottleneck_description: World-leading photoresist maker, strong across EUV, ArF-immersion and KrF resists; a top-tier holder of the advanced-photoresist choke-point that is roughly nine-tenths Japanese.
4186 JP.robotnik_notes: Advanced photoresist is a named frontier choke-point, with Japanese producers holding around nine-tenths of global supply, and TOK is one of the handful of top-tier makers alongside JSR, the overall leader, plus Shin-Etsu, Sumitomo and Fujifilm. Resist qualification at a leading-edge fab runs one to two years or more, so customers cannot swap resists mid-node, and the category's strategic status is proven by the 2019 Japan-Korea export-control episode. Every EUV layer of advanced logic and memory depends on it. It rates HIGH rather than CRITICAL because TOK shares the gate with JSR and others at the firm level, even though national concentration would tempt a higher call.

5384 JP.bottleneck_description: World leader in silicon-wafer final-polishing slurries and a leader in front-end-of-line CMP slurry; a concentrated niche upstream of every silicon wafer and advanced device.
5384 JP.robotnik_notes: Fujimi holds a dominant global share of silicon-wafer final-polishing agents and a majority of front-end-of-line CMP products, concentrated niches where its lines are the incumbent-qualified standard and slurry qualification is long and per-node. On the broader back-end CMP-slurry market it is only one of five, with Entegris, Resonac, DuPont and Merck as qualified alternatives, which is why it rates HIGH rather than CRITICAL. Advanced logic and memory require ever more CMP steps as nodes scale, so AI and leading-edge demand pulls Fujimi volume directly. The headline shares come from company figures relayed through an analyst source, hence medium confidence; named customers are not disclosed at a sourceable level and are left unstated rather than inferred.

RGTI.bottleneck_description: Full-stack superconducting quantum-computing company with an in-house superconducting-chip fab (Fab-1); pre-commercial, with no part of the stack yet dependent on it.
RGTI.key_customers: US Air Force Research Laboratory, DARPA, Amazon Braket (distribution)
RGTI.robotnik_notes: Quantum computing is pre-commercial research, and nothing in robotics, semiconductors, space or materials depends on Rigetti today; usage is experimental and revenue is immaterial. The field is crowded and contestable, with IBM, Google, IonQ, Quantinuum and others, and effectively no switching lock-in for users. Its in-house Fab-1, described as the first dedicated quantum foundry, is a genuine vertical-integration differentiator worth noting, but it is a capability Rigetti uses for itself rather than an input others must buy, so it creates no control point. Rated LOW with high confidence, the textbook pre-commercial case.

6680 HK.bottleneck_description: World's largest producer by volume of high-performance sintered NdFeB permanent magnets, used in EV traction motors, wind turbines and robotics; the leading operator inside China's magnet bloc.
6680 HK.key_suppliers: China Northern Rare Earth (NdPr feedstock), China Rare Earth Group (heavy rare earths), Hastings Technology Metals (feedstock stake)
6680 HK.robotnik_notes: China makes the overwhelming majority of high-performance NdFeB magnets and JL MAG is the largest single operator, deeply depended on across EV drivetrains, wind and, increasingly, humanoid-robot rotor components. Magnet supply is a genuine choke, but the concentration sits with China at the country and export-licence level rather than with JL MAG specifically; several large Chinese peers such as Zhongke Sanhuan, Ningbo Yunsheng and Zhenghai can supply the same grades subject to re-qualification. It therefore rates HIGH, alongside MP Materials, not CRITICAL, and the CRITICAL node is one tier upstream at its own feedstock supplier, China Northern Rare Earth. It sits directly in China's October 2025 magnet export-licensing regime and was among the first to obtain general export licences, so the controls raised its scarcity value rather than cutting it off. Its listed EV customers are sourced; a specific humanoid-robot customer such as Tesla Optimus is not, and is not asserted here.

000660 KS.bottleneck_description: Rated on whether an AI-accelerator builder can take its HBM demand elsewhere. Two other makers are qualified (Samsung, Micron), so the position is not CRITICAL, but SK Hynix is the category leader, first to each HBM generation and holding roughly two-thirds of the leading customer's allocation, and moving volume away means a multi-quarter requalification against a supplier the customer already prefers. Customers can leave and few do, which is what HIGH means.

005930 KS.bottleneck_description: Rated on its DRAM leadership, its peak position, not on HBM where it is a substitutable non-leader (peak-position ruling). Samsung is the number-one maker in the three-supplier DRAM oligopoly (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron); a memory buyer cannot leave that oligopoly, and requalifying volume away from the category leader is a multi-quarter, multi-billion undertaking. On HBM specifically Samsung lags SK Hynix and would rate lower, but the grade attaches to the strongest frontier position, which for Samsung is DRAM. Category-dominant with a costly-but-possible substitute, which is what HIGH means.

2454 TT.bottleneck_description: Peak position is premium and mainstream mobile SoCs, where MediaTek sits at Android parity with Qualcomm. A handset maker can move a design to Qualcomm, or occasionally in-house silicon, at a redesign-cycle cost, so the work would move rather than stop. A supplier customers weigh against a close rival rather than depend on, which is what MEDIUM means.

GFS.bottleneck_description: Rated on its trusted-foundry and RF-SOI niche, not its commodity mature nodes (peak-position ruling). GlobalFoundries is the US trusted-foundry supplier for defence and aerospace and a category leader in RF-SOI, where a qualified part carries a multi-year requalification and, for trusted-foundry work, a sole-accredited constraint; its mature nodes, where UMC and SMIC compete, would rate LOW alone. Rated on the niche it dominates, not the volume it competes for, which is what HIGH means.

600584.bottleneck_description: Peak position is outsourced assembly and test, where JCET is the number-three OSAT globally. A customer can move packaging and test among the OSATs (ASE, Amkor, Powertech) at a requalification cost; JCET is not the advanced-packaging chokepoint, which sits upstream at the leading-edge foundry. A supplier others can substitute at a switching cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

8046 TT.bottleneck_description: Peak position is ABF flip-chip substrates, an oligopoly of a handful of qualified makers (Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, AT&S, Nan Ya). A processor maker can move substrate orders to another qualified supplier at a requalification cost, and Nan Ya is the smaller end of the top tier rather than a sole source. A supplier customers can substitute at a switching cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

ATS AV.bottleneck_description: Peak position is high-end IC and ABF substrates, one of the small set of qualified makers serving leading-edge packaging (Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, AT&S). A customer can requalify substrate supply elsewhere in the oligopoly at a switching cost, so the work would move rather than stop. A supplier others can substitute at a redesign cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

7741 JP.bottleneck_description: Rated on EUV mask blanks (peak-position ruling), where Hoya and AGC hold roughly ninety per cent of supply between them and no third source is near qualification. A leading-edge fab cannot pattern EUV layers without qualified blanks and has no near-term second path outside the duopoly, so switching away is a multi-year undertaking with no ready alternative. A duopoly with no viable near-term substitute, one step short of sole-source, which is what HIGH means.

7911 JP.bottleneck_description: Peak position is merchant photomasks, a structurally concentrated three-maker market (Toppan, DNP, Photronics). A chipmaker that outsources masks can move among the merchant suppliers at a requalification cost, so supply is substitutable within a narrow field. A supplier customers can switch at a cost rather than depend on, which is what MEDIUM means.

7912 JP.bottleneck_description: Peak position is leading-edge merchant photomasks, including advanced-node EUV work, in the same three-maker merchant field as Toppan and Photronics. A customer can requalify mask supply with another merchant maker at a switching cost, so the position is substitutable within a concentrated field. A supplier others can substitute at a cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

6471 JP.bottleneck_description: Peak position is precision linear-motion components (ball screws and linear guides) qualified into semiconductor tools and high-precision robotics, where NSK is number three of a concentrated top tier (THK, HIWIN, NSK). A tool builder can design in a rival's qualified component at a requalification cost, and copy-exact stickiness raises that cost without removing the alternative. A supplier others can substitute at a switching cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

LIN.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is on-site industrial and specialty gases for fabs, supplied under roughly fifteen-year contracts from plant built on the customer's site and piped directly in. A committed fab cannot switch on-site supplier mid-contract at any price, and requalifying a new gas supply is a multi-year undertaking. A category-dominant position a customer cannot leave for years, which is what HIGH means.

AI FP.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is on-site and bulk fab gases on the same long-term on-site model as the other gas majors, physically locked to the customer's plant for the contract term. Switching supply is a multi-year requalification a committed fab cannot take mid-contract. A costly-but-locked category position, which is what HIGH means.

APD.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is on-site fab gases and helium supply on the long-term on-site contract model, piped from plant on the customer's site and not switchable mid-contract. Requalifying a new gas supplier is a multi-year undertaking. A category-dominant position a customer cannot leave for years, which is what HIGH means.

4091 JP.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is electronic specialty and on-site gases for Asian fabs on the same on-site contract model, physically locked to the customer's plant. A committed fab cannot switch mid-contract and requalification runs for years. A costly-but-locked category position, which is what HIGH means.

2802 JP.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is ABF, Ajinomoto Build-up Film, the sole-source dielectric insulating film used in essentially every flip-chip IC substrate. No qualified alternative exists: a substrate maker cannot pattern advanced build-up layers without it, at any price on any timeline. That is no viable substitute at all, the archetype of CRITICAL.

MTRN.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is beryllium and thin-film deposition (sputtering-target) materials, where Materion is a leading supplier but a customer can qualify an alternative source at a requalification cost. A supplier others can substitute at a switching cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

SIE GR.bottleneck_description: Rated on Siemens EDA and its Calibre platform, the de-facto standard for physical verification, sign-off and mask synthesis at the leading edge, not on the diversified automation and energy book (peak-position ruling). Calibre is one of the small set of firms that hold electronic-design automation between them, with no practical substitute in the tapeout flow; moving off it re-tools a fab's whole sign-off methodology over years. A category-dominant position with a costly-but-possible substitute, which is what HIGH means.

COHR.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is datacentre optical transceivers and photonics for AI fabric, plus SiC substrates. Coherent is a leading merchant supplier but competes with several qualified vendors, so a customer can requalify supply at a switching cost. A supplier others prefer rather than depend on, which is what MEDIUM means.

PENG.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is AI compute and memory-integration infrastructure (SMART Modular memory plus AI cluster build-out), a capable integrator in a competitive field where hyperscalers multi-source. The work would move rather than stop. A supplier substitutable at a redesign cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

6594.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is precision brushless and servo motors, where Nidec is the world's largest maker but a customer can design in a rival's qualified motor at a requalification cost. A supplier others can substitute at a switching cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

HEXAB SS.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is industrial metrology and measurement, where Hexagon is a category leader alongside Keyence and Renishaw. A customer can requalify onto a competing metrology platform at a switching cost, so supply is substitutable within a concentrated field. A supplier others can substitute at a cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

KOPN.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is microdisplays for defence and AR headsets, a designed-in component with real qualification barriers but multiple qualified alternatives for the next design cycle. A supplier substitutable at a redesign cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

NOC.bottleneck_description: Rated on solid rocket motors, where Northrop and L3Harris (Aerojet Rocketdyne) form the two-supplier US market, not on the diversified defence book (peak-position ruling). A launch or missile programme has exactly two qualified motor sources, and requalifying away from one is a multi-year undertaking. A category-dominant duopoly position with a costly-but-possible substitute, which is what HIGH means.

LHX.bottleneck_description: Rated on solid rocket motors, where L3Harris (Aerojet Rocketdyne) and Northrop form the two-supplier US market, not on the diversified defence book (peak-position ruling). A launch or missile programme has exactly two qualified motor sources, and requalifying away from one is a multi-year undertaking. A category-dominant duopoly position with a costly-but-possible substitute, which is what HIGH means.

012450 KS.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is space launch, where Hanwha Aerospace is Korea's national launch prime (Nuri/KSLV) and a growing satellite-launch integrator. It is a national champion in a contestable global launch market, so the position is strong but substitutable. A supplier others can substitute at a cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

ONDS.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is autonomous drone-in-a-box systems and industrial wireless for critical infrastructure, an early leader in a competitive autonomous-systems field where several vendors qualify. The work would move rather than stop. A supplier substitutable at a redesign cost, which is what MEDIUM means.

4004 JP.bottleneck_description: Peak frontier position is back-end and advanced-packaging materials, where Resonac is a top-three CMP slurry maker (its copper GPX series qualified at TSMC) and number two in epoxy moulding compound, and is investing in CoWoS, HBM and RDL planarization. These are oligopolistic positions where a fab can requalify onto a competing slurry or compound at a switching cost. A supplier others can substitute at a requalification cost, which is what MEDIUM means.
